en: In the *Aitareya Āraṇyaka*, one should touch the ground [with the mantra]: "O Agni, homage! O Ilā, homage! Homage to the seers, the makers of mantras, the lords of mantras; homage be to you, the gods. Be auspicious to us, most peaceful; be very gracious, O Sarasvatī; let not your sky be seen by us. Then: "O gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; O worshipful ones, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious.
With firm limbs and bodies, praising you, may we attain that lifespan ordained by the gods."
May Indra and Agni be auspicious to us with their protections; may Mitra and Varuṇa, to whom oblations are offered, be auspicious through our hymns.
May Indra and Soma be auspicious for our well-being and for health; may Indra and Pūṣan be auspicious to us in the winning of booty.
I praise the people of holy vows with newest songs—Mitra and Varuṇa, who grant favor.
May they come hither; may they listen here: those noble rulers, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Agni.
With what aid will he, the wonderful, ever-increasing friend, come to us?
With what most powerful host?
Which true one among the exhilarations, most bountiful, shall intoxicate you with the soma-juice?
[He] shall break open even the firmest wealth.
Be indeed our protector, O friend of us who sing your praises; may you come with a hundred aids.
O Earth, be pleasant, free from thorns, and a place of rest for us;
grant us wide-spreading shelter.
"The female mongoose has lips for a lid and teeth as its encircling rim;
mistress of all speech, may she cause sweet-sounding words to be uttered here"—this is the essence of speech.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!
Now begins the First Āraṇyaka.

Om. Now follows the Mahāvrata. Having slain Vṛtra, Indra indeed became great (*mahān*); because he became great, that became the Mahāvrata, and that is the reason for the Mahāvrata’s name as "the Great Vow. Regarding this day, some say one should perform two *ājya* chants, but it is settled that there is only one. One who desires success should use the chant beginning with *pra vo devāyāgnaye*. One who desires prosperity should use the chant beginning with *viśo viśo vo atithim*; for the subjects (*viśaḥ*) are indeed prosperity, and thus he becomes possessed of prosperity.

Regarding the word "guest" (*atithi*), they say that one should not treat him thus, for the guest is a lord who may come and go at will. However, regarding this, it has been said: "One should certainly do so. For he who truly exists, who attains preeminence—he indeed becomes a guest. People do not pay heed to hospitality for one who does not exist. Therefore, one may certainly do this if one desires. If he should perform this, he should first recite this triplet of verses beginning with "We have come to the greatest slayer of Vṛtra. For those who desire this day sit through the year [in expectation], and it is they who arrive.

These three triplets have the *anuṣṭubh* as their head. The *gāyatrī* is indeed the Brahman, and the *anuṣṭubh* is speech; thus, by means of the Brahman, he unites speech with it. "Agni has been awakened by the fuel of men"—this [is for one] desiring fame. "The Hotṛ has been born as a perceiver"—this [is for one] desiring offspring and cattle. 1.1.1.

"Agni, the men [kindle] with their thoughts from the two fire-sticks"—this [verse] one desiring food recites. Agni, indeed, is the eater of food. In other *ājya* offerings, they approach Agni as it were after a long time; but here they approach Agni from the very beginning, and thus he enjoys food from the very beginning and strikes away evil from the very beginning. "With the movement of their hands they generate him"—this contains the word "born" (*jāta*). From this day, indeed, the sacrificer is born; therefore it contains the word "born. These are four meters; cattle are four-footed, for the sake of obtaining cattle.

There are those three metres; for these worlds are threefold and threefold; it is for the conquest of these very worlds. There are two metres; it is for support alone. Man indeed has two feet, and cattle have four feet; he thus establishes the sacrificer, who has two feet, among the four-footed cattle.

By reciting them in reverse order, they become twenty-five; for this person consists of twenty-five parts: ten fingers of the hands, ten toes of the feet, two thighs, two arms, and the self itself as the twenty-fifth. He thus consecrates this very self as the twenty-fifth. Moreover, this day is indeed twenty-five-fold, and the Stoma of this day is twenty-five-fold; thus he proceeds from like unto like. Therefore, there are exactly two sets of twenty-five.

Those [verses] are thirty minus one syllable, being three times the first [verse] and three times the last [verse]. The *virāj* consists of thirty syllables; for in what is deficient, seed is infused; in what is deficient, the vital breaths are established; in what is deficient, food is established. This is for the attainment of these desires. He who knows thus attains these desires. They result in the *bṛhatī* and the *virāj* meters, which are the perfection of this day; moreover, they result in the *anuṣṭubh*, for the *ājya* hymns have the *anuṣṭubh* as their abode. 1.1.2.

"One should make the *prauga* a *gāyatra*," they say; "the *gāyatrī* is indeed splendor and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); he becomes splendid and possessed of spiritual luster. "One should make the *prauga* an *auṣṇiha*," they say; "the *uṣṇih* is indeed life; he becomes long-lived."

"One should make the *prauga* in the *anuṣṭubh* metre," they say, "for the *anuṣṭubh* is the nobility (*kṣattra*); it is for the attainment of nobility. "One should make the *prauga* in the *bṛhatī* metre," they say, "for the *bṛhatī* is prosperity; one becomes prosperous. "One should make the *prauga* in the *paṅkti* metre," they say, "for the *paṅkti* is food; one becomes possessed of food. "One should make the *prauga* in the *triṣṭubh* metre," they say, "for the *triṣṭubh* is vigor; one becomes vigorous. "One should make the *prauga* in the *jagatī* metre," they say, "for cattle are of the *jagatī* nature; one becomes possessed of cattle. Thus it is said.

"Therefore, one should indeed perform the Gāyatra; for the Gāyatrī is the Brahman, and that day is the Brahman. By means of the Brahman, one thus attains the Brahman. "Furthermore, it is the Mādhucchandasa. "Madhucchandas used to offer honey (*madhu*) to the seers; that is why Madhucchandas has his name 'Madhucchandas'. "Moreover, honey is indeed food; honey is everything; honey is all desires. Therefore, when he recites the Mādhucchandasa, it is for the attainment of all desires."

"He who knows thus obtains all desires. This [rite] belongs to a single day (*ekāha*) and is rich in form; for on this day, many various prohibitions (*vāraṇa*) are performed for the sake of peace (*śānti*). Indeed, the *ekāha* is peace and stability; thus, in the end, they find firm support in that very peace and stability. He who knows thus finds firm support, as do those for whom the Hotṛ, knowing this, recites it.
Thus ends the third section of the first chapter of the first Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyakaṇḍa. || 1.1.3 ||

"O Vāyu, come hither, O beautiful one; these Somas have been prepared"—this day is indeed "prepared" (araṃ) for both the sacrificer and the gods. This day becomes truly prepared for him who knows this, as well as for those for whom the Hotṛ, knowing this, recites it. "O Indra and Vāyu, these [Somas] are pressed; come to the prepared [place]"—that which is "prepared" (niṣkṛta) is that which is consecrated (saṃskṛta). Indra and Vāyu come to what has been consecrated for him who knows this, as well as for those for whom the Hotṛ, knowing this, recites it.

"I invoke Mitra of purified skill; may he perfect the butter-smeared prayer"—for the prayer is indeed speech, and the butter-smeared is speech. He who knows this places speech within himself, as well as for those for whom the Hotṛ, knowing thus, recites this. "The Aśvins, [bring] the nourishing offerings"—for the offerings are indeed food, [recited] for the attainment of food. "Come, O you whose path is red"—verily, the Aśvins come to his sacrifice, he who knows this, and for whom the Hotṛ, knowing thus, recites this.

"O Indra, come with brilliant luster; O Indra, come, impelled by our prayer; O Indra, come, hastening"—thus he recites "Come! Come! Indra indeed comes to him who knows this, as well as to those for whom the Hotṛ, knowing this, recites this. "The protectors, the sustainers of men, all you gods, come hither"—thus [he recites]. All the gods indeed come to his call who knows this, as well as to those for whom the Hotṛ, knowing this, recites this.

"When he says, 'The givers [have given] the pressed juice of the giver,' he thereby says, 'The givers [have given] the pressed juice of the giver. The gods grant him that desire for which he recites this; so it is for one who knows thus, and for those for whom the Hotṛ, knowing thus, recites this. 'May the purifying Sarasvatī, rich in wisdom, desire our sacrifice'—for she who is rich in wisdom is indeed Speech. He places speech within him who knows thus, and for those for whom the Hotṛ, knowing thus, recites this."

When he says, "May it desire the sacrifice," he thereby means, "May it carry the sacrifice. These [verses], by being recited in the *parācī* manner, become twenty-one; this person consists of twenty-one—the ten fingers of the hands, the ten toes of the feet, and the self as the twenty-first—and thus he consecrates this very self as the twenty-first.

There are three repetitions of the first [verse] and three of the last; thus they become twenty-five. The self (ātman) is twenty-fivefold; Prajāpati is twenty-fivefold: ten fingers of the hands, ten toes of the feet, two thighs, two arms, and the self itself is the twenty-fifth. He thereby consecrates this self as twenty-fivefold. Moreover, this day is twenty-fivefold, and the stoma of this day is twenty-fivefold; thus he proceeds from like unto like. Therefore, there are indeed two sets of twenty-five. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the fourth section of the first chapter in the first Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyakāṇḍa. Thus ends the first chapter of the first Āraṇyaka in the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyakāṇḍa.

"Come to us as to a chariot for aid; O Vasu, this pressed juice," these are the *pratipad* and *anucara* of the *marutvatīya* [śastra]. They belong to the one-day (*aikāhika*) sacrifice and are rich in form. Indeed, on this day much that is forbidden is performed; it is for the sake of pacification. The one-day sacrifice is indeed peace and a firm foundation. Thus, in the end, they find support in peace and in that foundation. He who knows this finds support, as do those for whom the Hotṛ, knowing thus, recites this.

"O Indra, come nearer; let the impulsion come through thy powers, [to those] who offer thee hymns"—this day is indeed characterized by hymns (*uktha*); thus, this form is rich in hymns, which is the characteristic form of this day. "May Brahmanaspati advance toward the hero"—this form is rich in heroes; thus, this form is the characteristic form of this day. "Arise, O Brahmanaspati, for heroic power"—this form is rich in heroic power; thus, this form is the characteristic form of this day.

"Now indeed Brahmanaspati speaks the mantra worthy of praise"—this day is indeed a *uktha* (praise-chant), and this form, being rich in *ukthas*, is the characteristic form of this day. "Agni is the leader, he is the slayer of Vṛtra"—this is the *vārtraghna* (Vṛtra-slaying) form of Indra; this day belongs to Indra, and this form is the characteristic form of this day. "O Soma, you have become one of good wisdom through your powers; you are a bull by your bull-like deeds and greatness"—this contains the word *vṛṣan* (bull); the form of Indra is that of Indra, and this day belongs to Indra, and this form is the characteristic form of this day.

“They moisten the waters like a steed for rain; they lead forth the racer”—for the form of Indra is indeed possessed of speed (*vājimat*), and this day belongs to Indra; thus it is the form of this day. And: “They milk the fountain that thunders, the inexhaustible”—for the form of Indra is indeed thundering, and this day belongs to Indra; thus it is the form of this day. And: “Forward to you, for the great Indra”—for what is great is indeed vast (*bṛhat*); the form of this day is richly endowed with greatness (*mahadvat*). Thus it is the form of this day.

"Sing the *bṛhat* for Indra"—for what is *bṛhat* (great) is indeed *mahat* (vast), and this day is richly endowed with the form of *mahat*; such is its form. "No one has overturned the chariot of Sudās, nor has he caused it to stop"—this is richly endowed with the forms of being overturned and coming to rest; such is the form of this day. He recites all the *pragāthas* for the attainment of all the days, all the *ukthas*, all the *pṛṣṭhas*, all the *śastras*, all the *praugas*, and all the *savanas*.
Thus ends the first section of the second chapter in the first Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyakāṇḍa. || 1 ||

"In the absence of these [verses], the Jaritṛ [Sāman] with its impetus proclaims, 'Truth is the path of the righteous' (*satyadhvṛtam*). This day is indeed truth; it is rich in the form of truth—this is the form of this day. Regarding that, it is the *Vasukra*: Vasukra is indeed Brahman; this day is Brahman; thus, by means of Brahman, one attains Brahman.

Regarding this they say: "Now, why does one begin this Marutvatīya with the Vāsukra [hymn]? [The answer is: "For no one other than Vāsukra has ever raised up the Marutvatīya; he did not fail in it. Therefore, one begins this Marutvatīya with the Vāsukra. He recites that which is unexpressed (anirukta), pertaining to Prajāpati; for Prajāpati is indeed unexpressed, and it is for the attainment of Prajāpati. He mentions Indra once; thereby he does not fall away from the form of Indra.

"He drinks the Soma, O fierce one, for whom [he is] a slayer"—thus he recites. "O Indra, being praised, [open] the great stall of cattle"—this, containing the word *mahi* (great), is the form-perfection that is the characteristic form of this day. Now, as for the Bhāradvāja hymn: Bharadvāja was indeed the most learned among the seers (*ṛṣis*), the longest-lived, and the most ascetic. By means of this hymn, he drove away evil. Therefore, when he recites the Bhāradvāja hymn, it is for the purpose of driving away evil, thinking, "May I be learned, long-lived, and ascetic. For this reason, he recites the Bhāradvāja hymn.

"With what [splendor] are they fair, of equal age, and dark-complexioned?"—thus he recites. "They pray and they respond with the *uktha*," for this day is indeed an *uktha*-day; it possesses the form of an *uktha*, and this is the characteristic form of this day. Now, this is the *Kayāśubhīya* hymn. This *Kayāśubhīya* is a hymn of recognition and continuity. By means of this, Indra, Agastya, and the Maruts reached a mutual understanding. Therefore, when he recites the *Kayāśubhīya*, it is for the sake of concord.

"That [verse] is life-giving; he for whom one has affection should indeed perform this *Kayāśubhīya* for him. Thus it is said. He recites, "O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, the bull, for the battle... He recites, "O Indra, the bull," because the form of Indra is "possessing the bull" (*vṛṣaṇvat*), and this day belongs to Indra; thus it is the form of this day. That [hymn] belongs to Viśvāmitra. For Viśvāmitra was indeed the friend of all. He for whom one knows this becomes the friend of all, as does he for whom the Hotṛ, knowing this, recites it.

"Thou hast been born fierce for the sake of conquering force"—this is the *Nivid* hymn belonging to the one-day sacrifice (*aikāhika*), rich in form. Indeed, on this day, many various things that are to be avoided are performed; it is for the sake of pacification. For the one-day sacrifice is peace and stability. Thus, they finally find their support in peace and stability. He who knows this finds support, as do those for whom the Hotṛ, knowing thus, recites this.

By counting them in reverse order, they become ninety-seven. Of those, the ninety consist of three sets of thirty, which are *virāj* verses; as for the seven that remain over, they constitute the very praise of the *sāptya*. Thus, by repeating the first verse three times and the last verse three times, they become one hundred and one. There are five fingers with four joints each, two armpits, the two arms, the axle, and the shoulder-blade—that makes twenty-five; the other limbs are likewise twenty-five each, making a hundred, and the self (*ātman*) is the one hundred and first.

"Whatever life-span, sensory power, vigor, and brilliance there are in those hundred [years], the sacrificer becomes established in that one-hundred-and-first life-span, sensory power, vigor, and brilliance. These [verses] culminate in the *triṣṭubh* meter, for the midday pressing is indeed of the *triṣṭubh* nature. Thus ends the second section of the second chapter in the first *Āraṇyaka* of the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa*.

Regarding this they say: "What is the 'swinging' (*preṅkha*) nature of the swing? This very one who blows is the swing, for he swings through these worlds; that is the swinging nature of the swing. They say there should be a single plank, for this wind blows as a single entity, according to its form. But that is not to be heeded. They say there should be three planks, for these three worlds are threefold, according to their form. But that too is not to be heeded.

"There should be exactly two, for these two worlds are seen as if most closely joined; that space which is between them is the intermediate world (antarikṣaloka). Therefore, there should be exactly two. "They should be made of udumbara wood; the udumbara is indeed vigor and food. This is for the attainment of vigor and food. "They should be raised up in the middle; for in the middle, offspring thrive upon food. Thus, he places the sacrificer in the very midst of food."

"There are two kinds of ropes, those for the right side and those for the left. For some animals the ropes are on the right, and for others they are on the left. As to why there are two kinds of ropes: it is for the attainment of both types of animals. They should be made of *darbha* grass; for *darbha* is the most pure among plants, therefore they should be made of *darbha*. Thus ends the third section of the second chapter of the first Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyakakāṇḍa.

"An arm's length above the ground should be the swing," they say, "for by this much the heavenly worlds are measured"; but that is not to be heeded. "It should be a span's length," they say, "for by this much the vital breaths are measured"; but that is not to be heeded. "It should be the size of a fist," [they say]; "for by this much all food is prepared, and by this much all food is encompassed; therefore it should be exactly the size of a fist."

"One should mount the swing facing west from the east," they say, "in accordance with the form of him who shines yonder; for he indeed mounts these worlds facing west from the east. But that is not to be heeded. "One should mount it crosswise," they say, "for they mount a horse crosswise; thus we shall obtain all our desires. But that too is not to be heeded.

"One should mount it lengthwise," they say, "for they mount a boat lengthwise; this swing is indeed a boat for traveling to heaven. Therefore, one should mount it only lengthwise. "One should touch it with the chin," [they say], "for the parrot mounts a tree in this manner, and it is the most voracious among birds. Therefore, one should touch it with the chin. "One should mount it with the arms," [they say], "for the hawk settles upon birds in this manner, and it is the most powerful among birds. Therefore, one should mount it with the arms."

"One should not cut off its foot, lest one cut off its foundation," so it is said. The Hotṛ ascends the swing (*preṅkha*), and the Udgātṛ ascends the throne-seat (*āsandi*) made of *udumbara* wood. The swing is indeed male, and the throne-seat is female; that is a pair. Thus, at the beginning of the *uktha*, he creates a pair for the sake of procreation. He who knows this is propagated with offspring and cattle. Now, the swing is indeed food, and the throne-seat is prosperity; thus they both ascend after food and prosperity.

"The *hotrakas*, together with the *brahmán*, mount the seats," it is said. Or rather, "the plants and trees bear fruit after having fully grown. Therefore, when they all mount [the seats] on this day, they mount upon prosperity, vigor, and food; it is for the attainment of vigor and food. "One should descend after uttering the *vaṣaṭ*-call," so they say; but that is not to be heeded, for that honor is not truly performed which one does while not looking at the person [to whom it is directed].

"One should descend while holding the sacrificial food (bhakṣa)," so they say; "but that should not be heeded, for that is no honor which one performs for a guest without looking at him. "One should descend after having looked at the sacrificial food; this indeed is the honor which one performs when one looks upon him. Therefore, one should descend only after having looked at the sacrificial food. "One should descend facing east; for the seed of the gods is generated in the east. Therefore, one should descend facing east. Thus he should descend.
Thus ends the fourth section in the second chapter of the first Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyakāṇḍa. Thus ends the second chapter in the first Āraṇyaka of the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyakāṇḍa.

"One should begin this day with the *hiṅkāra*," they say. "The *hiṅkāra* is indeed Brahman; that day is Brahman. He who knows thus attains Brahman by means of Brahman. "In that one begins with the *hiṅkāra*—the *hiṅkāra* is indeed a male and the *ṛc* is a female—it creates a union at the beginning of the hymn (*uktha*) for the sake of procreation. He who knows thus is procreated with offspring and cattle."

Moreover, as to why one should commence with the *hiṃkāra*: just as a spade is, so is the *hiṃkāra* of the Brahman. Whatever one desires to dig up with a spade, one digs it up; even so, whatever desire one desires, he who knows this digs it up by means of the *hiṃkāra*.

Or rather, as for why one should commence with the *hiṃkāra*: this *hiṃkāra* is the separation of speech into that which is divine and that which is human. When he commences after uttering the *hiṃkāra*, he thereby separates speech itself into the divine and the human. Thus ends the first section of the third chapter of the first Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.

Regarding this, they say: "What is the opening verse (*pratipad*) of this day? One should reply: "Mind and speech. "All other desires are supported by them; it yields all other desires. Indeed, all desires are supported in the mind, for with the mind one meditates upon all desires. "All desires are indeed supported in him who knows thus. Speech indeed yields all desires, for with speech one speaks of all desires. "Speech yields all desires for him who knows thus."

Regarding this, they say: "One should not enter upon this day directly with a *ṛc*, nor with a *yajus*, nor with a *sāman*; one should not go forth from the *ṛc*, nor from the *yajus*, nor from the *sāman*. Therefore, one should mutter these *vyāhṛtis* beforehand. These *vyāhṛtis*—namely *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*—are indeed the three Vedas: *bhūḥ* is the *Ṛgveda*, *bhuvaḥ* is the *Yajurveda*, and *svaḥ* is the *Sāmaveda*. Thus, one does not enter upon it directly with a *ṛc*, nor with a *yajus*, nor with a *sāman*; one goes forth neither from the *ṛc*, nor from the *yajus*, nor from the *sāman*.
Thus ends the second section of the third chapter in the first Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa Āraṇyakakāṇḍa.

"He understands it as 'that' or as 'this'; he understands food as food indeed. Prajāpati first uttered this speech consisting of one syllable and two syllables: "tat" and "tāt. In the same way, a child who speaks for the first time utters speech consisting of one syllable and two syllables: "tat" and "tāt. By that very speech, "tat-tatavatī," he understands. This has been stated by the Seer (Ṛṣi): *Note: The phrase "tat-tatavatyā" is interpreted here as "that which possesses the quality of being 'tat' (that/this). The text reflects the Vedic view on the origin of language and its connection to the understanding of reality.*

"Bṛhaspati, the first peak of speech"—for this is indeed the first peak of speech. "When they went forth, assuming their names"—for by means of speech, names are established. "That which was their best, that which was unassailable"—for this is indeed the best, and this is unassailable. "By love, that which was hidden in their secret cave has been revealed"—this refers to the self (adhyātma): these deities are hidden within the self, while those [external] deities are revealed as the divine realm (adhidaivata); this is what is meant.
Thus ends the third section of the third chapter of the first Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyakāṇḍa. || 3 ||

"That indeed was the eldest among beings"—with these words he begins; for this [Agni] is indeed the eldest among beings. "From whence he was born fierce and brilliant in manliness"—for from there he was born fierce and brilliant in manliness. "As soon as born, he overcomes his enemies"—for as soon as he was born, he struck away evil. "Him whom all the helpers rejoice in"—the "all" are indeed the elements (bhūtāni) and the "helpers" (ūmāḥ); they rejoice after him, crying out, "He has risen! He has risen!"

"Growing strong in power, possessing abundant vigor"—this indeed means "growing strong in power, possessing abundant vigor. "He strikes fear into the Dāsa enemy"—this means he instills dread in the Dāsa foe. "He wins both the solid and the liquid"—by this he means both that which has life and that which is lifeless. "They cry out together for thee at the offerings during the exhilarations"—by this he means "everything is under thy control."

"In all [beings] they encompass your will"—by this he means: "All these beings, all minds, and all wills encompass you. "When these two become three times," he says; for when two exist as a pair, they procreate for the sake of generation. He who knows thus is procreated with offspring and cattle.

"Mix the sweet with the sweeter; for the sweet is indeed the couple, and the offspring is the sweet; thus, by means of the couple, he unites the offspring. "Strike that honey with honey; for honey is indeed the couple, and the offspring is honey; thus, by means of the couple, he strikes at the offspring. This has been stated by the Seer: "When he extended his own body within the body," by which he means this very physical body composed of the *chandas* meters.

"Let the body itself be the medicine for the body"—by this he means that this [body] consists of the *chandas* (metres). Of that [body], those which are eight syllables are the *gāyatrī*; those which are eleven are the *triṣṭubh*; those which are twelve are the *jagatī*; and those which are ten are the *virāj*. It is established upon these three metres in their ten-syllable forms. "Puruṣa" has three syllables; it is thus established in the *virāj*.

"Verily, all these meters are those which have the *virāj* as their fourth; and for one who knows thus, this day becomes entered upon by means of all the meters. Thus ends the fourth section in the third chapter of the first Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.

"He dwells with the *nada* (roaring sound); man indeed is the *nada*, therefore every man when speaking seems to be roaring. "The *nada* of the *odati*s," [so it is said]. The *odati*s are the waters; those which are celestial, for they moisten (*undanti*) all this; the *odati*s are the waters; those which are in the mouth, for they moisten all this food. "The *nada* of the *yoyuvati*s," [so it is said]. The *yoyuvati*s are the waters; those which are in the intermediate space, for they seem to float (*poplūyante*); the *yoyuvati*s are the waters; those which sweat, for they seem to glide (*sarīsṛpyante*).

"O inviolable ones, [I praise] you as the lord of your [waters]"—thus [it is said]. Indeed, the waters are the inviolable ones; they are the inviolable ones which are born from the smoke of Agni, and they are the inviolable ones which are emitted from the penis. "May you seek after the milch-cows"—thus [it is said]. The waters indeed are the milch-cows, for they satisfy (dhinvanti) all this; when he says "seek after," he means "become a mistress. He interchanges the *triṣṭubh* and the *anuṣṭubh*; the *triṣṭubh* is indeed the male and the *anuṣṭubh* is the female. That is a union; therefore, even when a man has obtained a wife, he considers himself, as it were, more complete.

These, repeated three times with the first [verse], become twenty-five; the self (ātman) is twenty-five-fold, Prajāpati is twenty-five-fold: ten fingers of the hands, ten toes of the feet, two thighs, two arms, and the self itself is the twenty-fifth. He thus prepares this self as twenty-five-fold. Moreover, this day is twenty-five-fold, and the Stoma of this day is twenty-five-fold; thus he proceeds from like unto like. Therefore, there are indeed two sets of twenty-five. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the fifth section in the third chapter of the first Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka.

He understands it as "tat" or "tattat"; he understands it as food, for that is indeed food. Prajāpati first uttered this very speech, consisting of one syllable or two syllables: "tat" and "tāt. In the same way, a child, when first speaking, utters speech consisting of one syllable or two syllables: "tat" and "tāt. By means of that very speech, which contains the essence of "tat," he attains it. This has been said by the Seer: "O Bṛhaspati, the first peak of speech"—for this is indeed the first peak of speech.

"Those who, assuming names, strove forth"—for by speech indeed are names assumed. "That which was their best, that which was unassailable"—this is indeed the best, this is the unassailable. "By love (preṇā) it was placed within them as a secret, yet made manifest"—this refers to the secret [aspect] with respect to the self (*adhyātma*), namely these deities; and that which is manifest refers to the divine sphere (*adhidaivata*). This is what is meant. Thus ends the sixth section of the third chapter of the first Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa Āraṇyaka.

"That indeed was the eldest among beings"—with these words he begins; for what is the eldest, that is the great, and the form of this day is rich in greatness. "O Maghavan, that fame of yours through your majesty"—this form of this day is rich in greatness. "For even more, for heroic deeds"—this form of this day is rich in heroism.

"O men, you [praise] you, the most manly, with songs and hymns"—this day is indeed a hymn; it possesses the form of a hymn, which is the characteristic form of this day. He distributes [the verses] with deficient syllables in the first feet; for seed is poured into what is deficient, vital breaths are established in what is deficient, and food is established in what is deficient. For the attainment of these desires, he who knows thus attains these desires.

There are two [verses] of ten syllables each for the attainment of both kinds of food. With the words "that which has feet" and "that which is footless," there are eighteen syllables; of these, ten are the nine vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and the self (*ātman*) is the tenth. That is the consecration of the self. Eight by eight they are raised up; he attains whatever he desires who knows thus. Thus ends the seventh section in the third chapter of the first *Āraṇyaka* of the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa*.

"He dwells with the *nada* (sound); the breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the *nada*; therefore, the breath, sounding, makes everything sound as it were. "O you who flow toward the *nada*," this *uṣṇih* verse consists of syllables and is an *anuṣṭubh* in its feet; the *uṣṇih* is life-breath (*āyus*) and the *anuṣṭubh* is speech (*vāc*); thus he bestows both life-breath and speech upon him.

These, repeated three times with the first verse, become twenty-five. The self is twenty-five-fold; Prajāpati is twenty-five-fold: ten fingers of the hands, ten toes of the feet, two thighs, two [shanks], and the voice is the self itself as the twenty-fifth. He thus prepares this self as twenty-five-fold. Moreover, this day is twenty-five-fold, and the *stoma* of this day is twenty-five-fold; thus he proceeds from like unto like. Therefore, indeed, there are twenty-five; such is the twenty-five-fold division with respect to the self (*adhyātma*).

Now, with respect to the deities: sight, hearing, mind, speech, and breath—these five deities have entered this person; and indeed, these five deities have entered this person. Thus, from the hair to the nails, he is obtained in his entirety, with all his limbs. Therefore, all beings, down to the ants, are born already complete. This has been said by the Seer: "The fifteen-fold hymns in a thousand ways"—for there are indeed five decades.

"As vast as heaven and earth, so vast is this"—for as great as heaven and earth are, so great is the Self. "A thousandfold are the greatnesses, a thousand"—thus he rejoices in and magnifies the hymns (*ukthas*). "As far as Brahman extends, so far extends speech"—for wherever there is Brahman, there is speech, and wherever there is speech, there is Brahman; this is what is meant by that. Of these hymns (*sūktas*), the first consists of nine verses; for there are nine vital breaths (*prāṇas*), and it serves for the establishment of the vital breaths.

"It consists of six verses; for there are six seasons, [it serves] for the attainment of the seasons. "It consists of five verses; the *paṅkti* has five feet, and the *paṅkti* is indeed food, [it serves] for the securing of food," and so forth. "It consists of three verses; for these worlds are threefold, [it serves] for the conquest of these very worlds. These [verses] culminate in the *bṛhatī* metre, which is immortality and the world of the gods; this is the Self. Thus, one who knows this, by means of this very attainment, attains the immortal Self; he truly attains it.

Thus ends the eighth section (khaṇḍa) of the third chapter (adhyāya) of the first Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyakāṇḍa. Thus ends the third chapter (adhyāya) of the first Āraṇyaka in the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyakāṇḍa.

Now begins the fourth chapter of the first Āraṇyaka. 1.4.1: Now follows the *sūdadohas* verse. The *sūdadohas* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*); by means of the vital breath, he joins together the joints. Next, they explain the neck-vertebrae according to the meters, beginning with the *uṣṇih*. Then follows the *sūdadohas* verse: the *sūdadohas* is indeed the vital breath; by means of the vital breath, he joins together the joints.

Now, therefore, follows the Head. It occurs in *gāyatrī* verses; for the *gāyatrī* is the foremost of the meters, and the head is the foremost of the limbs. It occurs in verses containing the word "arka"; for Agni is indeed the *arka*. There are nine of these; for the head consists of nine skull-bones. He recites the tenth verse; that one serves as the skin and the hair. Moreover, it is for the sake of exceeding the *stoma*. These two *stomas* are the *trivṛt* and the *gāyatra* meter. Following the progeny of these two *stoma*-meters, everything here that exists is produced for the sake of procreation.

"Thus, he who knows this is procreated with offspring and cattle. Then follows the Sūdadohas verse: "The Sūdadohas is indeed the vital breath; by the vital breath he joins the joints together. Now, therefore, regarding the *vijava* verses: they are *virāj* meters. Therefore, one man says to another who is struggling, "Truly, you shine among us; you indeed support our necks. Or, when people are running, those who are most robust and most fit for food are seen to be the most excellent; for the *virāj* is food, and food is vigor.

Now, therefore, follows the right wing: this world, this Agni, that speech, that Rathantara, that Vasiṣṭha—these are the hundred; these are the six powers. They constitute a Paṅkti for the attainment of desires, for stability, and for the sake of food. Thus it is said.

Now follows the subsequent section: That world is yonder sun; that is the mind; that is the Bṛhat; that is Bharadvāja; that is the hundred; those are the six powers. This is indeed a *saṃpāta* [conjunction] for the attainment of desires, for stability, and for the sake of food—this is the *paṅkti* [pentad]. These two [sāmans] are deficient and redundant: the Bṛhat is the male, the Rathantara is the female; what is redundant belongs to the male, and what is deficient belongs to the female; therefore [they are so].

"Deficiency and excess occur; for indeed, by one [verse], Suparṇa’s right wing is greater. Therefore, the right wing becomes larger by one ṛc. Then there is the *sūdadohas* verse; the *sūdadohas* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*); with the vital breath he joins the joints together. Now, therefore, follows the tail: those twenty-one two-footed verses exist, for these twenty-one downward-pointing feathers of Suparṇa exist.

"Moreover, the twenty-one-fold is indeed the foundation of the *stomas*, and the foundation is the tail of birds. He recites the twenty-two-fold; thus the form of the two foundations is created. Therefore, all birds establish themselves on their tails, and having established themselves on their tails, they fly up; for the tail is the foundation.

This very person is established upon these two twenty-two-syllable feet, which are two *virāj* verses consisting of two tens. That which is his form as a bird (*suparṇa*) is for the attainment of his desires; and that which is his form as a human (*puruṣa*) is for his prosperity, glory, food, and honor.

Now [comes] the *sūdadohas*, then the *dhāyyā*, then the *sūdadohas*. The *sūdadohas* is indeed a male, and the *dhāyyā* is a female. Therefore, he recites the *dhāyyā* on both sides of the *sūdadohas*. For this reason, the seed, once emitted into two [receptacles], attains unity. Indeed, it is from the female that one is born; from her comes progeny. Therefore, he recites this [the *dhāyyā*] here. Thus ends the second section of the fourth chapter in the first Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa Āraṇyaka.

"He recites the Gāyatrī consisting of eighty-three triplets. This world is indeed the Gāyatrī consisting of eighty-three triplets. Whatever glory, whatever greatness, whatever union, whatever food, and whatever honor there is in this world—that I may attain, that I may obtain, that I may secure for myself, and that it may be mine—[he thinks]. Then follows the Sūdadohas verse. The Sūdadohas is indeed the vital breath; by means of the vital breath he connects this world [with the next]."

He recites the eighty-three triplets of the Bṛhatī metre. The eighty-three triplets of the Bṛhatī are indeed the intermediate world. Whatever glory, whatever greatness, whatever union, whatever food, and whatever honor there is in the intermediate world—that he may attain, that he may win, that he may secure for himself, and that it may be his—[he recites them]. Then follows the Sūdadohas verse. The Sūdadohas is indeed the vital breath; by means of the vital breath, he connects the intermediate world [with the next].

He recites the eighty-three triplets in the *auṣṇiha* meter. The sky, that world above, is indeed the *auṣṇiha* triplet-series of eighty-three. Whatever glory, whatever greatness, whatever union, whatever food, whatever honor, and whatever divinity belongs to the gods in that world—that may I attain, that may I reach, that may I secure for myself; may it be mine. Then follows the *sūdadohas* verse. The *sūdadohas* is indeed breath; by means of breath he connects that world, he connects it. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the third section of the fourth chapter in the first Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyakāṇḍa. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the first Āraṇyaka of the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyakāṇḍa.

Now begins the fifth chapter of the first Āraṇyaka; therein is the first section (the twentieth). He recites the *vaśa* [verse], thinking, "May all this be under my control. These [verses] become twenty-one, for there are twenty-one transformations within the belly. Moreover, the twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*) is indeed the foundation of the *stomas*, and the belly is the foundation of food. They consist of various meters (*vicchandasas*), for that which is within is, as it were, diverse—both smaller and larger.

He recites them with the *praṇava*, according to the meters, and as they occur; for the internal [recitation] is, as it were, occurring as it happens—sometimes shorter, sometimes longer. Then follows the *sūdadohas*: the *sūdadohas* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*); by means of the vital breath he joins the joints together.

"Therefore, having recited [the hymn] twelve times, he releases her there; for these vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are of twelve kinds: seven in the head, two in the breasts, and three downward. Here indeed the vital breaths are obtained, here they are refined; therefore he releases her there. "O Indra and Agni, you two well for us..."—this belongs to Indra and Agni; the thighs and the knees are the foundation.

"These [verses] consist of six feet; it is for the sake of stability, for man is indeed two-footed and cattle are four-footed; he thus establishes the two-footed sacrificer among the four-footed cattle. The second [verse] consists of seven feet; he makes it both a *gāyatrī* and an *anuṣṭubh*. The *gāyatrī* is indeed the Brahman and the *anuṣṭubh* is speech; by means of the Brahman, he thus unites speech.

He recites the *triṣṭubh* at the end; the *triṣṭubh* is indeed vigor. By means of vigor, he thus encompasses the cattle. Therefore, the cattle stand in attendance upon vigor, both in their movement and in their rising up. Thus ends the first section of the fifth chapter in the first *Āraṇyaka* of the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa*.

"In the *niṣkevalya* litany for Indra, beginning with *pra vo mahe mandamānāyāndhasaḥ*, these verses are in the *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* meters. Regarding this, they ask: "Why then does he place the *nivid* in *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* verses? [The answer is: "For indeed, no single meter of this day has supported the *nivid*, nor has any encompassed it; therefore, he places the *nivid* in *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* verses. One should know that this day possesses three *nivid*s: the *vaśa* is a *nivid*, the *vālakhilyās* are a *nivid*, and the *nivid* itself is a *nivid*; thus one should know that this day possesses three *nivid*s.

"Now, [the hymn] 'By the wood, O Vāyu, has he been placed; he who, as soon as born, was the first mindful one'—in these two [verses], there is the line 'when their thoughts met upon the food,' for the attainment of food. Then follows the insertion: between these [hymns], they insert as many verses of *daśatis* consisting of *triṣṭubhs* and *jagatīs* dedicated to Indra as they insert; for as many years beyond their [normal] lifespan do they live by this very insertion; through this insertion, indeed, life is obtained."

"He recites the *Sajanīya* with the thought, 'May cattle bring me offspring. He recites the *Tārkṣya*; the *Tārkṣya* is indeed a means of well-being (*svastyayana*), so he effects well-being for the sake of safety. He recites the *Ekapadā* with the thought, 'May I become all this as one,' and also, 'May I attain the entire creation of meters.'"

"Indra have all strengthened"—these are the seven verses with appended lines; he appends these seven. For there are indeed seven vital breaths in the head; thus he places the vital breaths in the head. He does not append the eighth, thinking, "Speech is the eighth; let it not be appended to the vital breaths by me. Therefore, that speech, though having the same abode as the vital breaths, is not actually appended to them. He recites the Virāj verses; for the Virājs are food, and it is for the attainment of food.

"Indram viśvā avīvṛdhan"—these are the seven verses with appended lines (*anuṣaṅga*); he appends these seven. For there are indeed seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in the head; thus he places the vital breaths in the head. He does not append the eighth verse, thinking, "Speech is the eighth; let it not be appended to the vital breaths. Therefore, that speech, though having the same abode as the vital breaths, is not appended to them. He recites the *virāj* verses; the *virāj*s are indeed food, for the attainment of food. He concludes with a verse belonging to Vasiṣṭha, thinking, "May I be a Vasiṣṭha."

"This hymn is for the great and fierce one," [he says] with a verse containing the word "great" (*mahat*), thus it is rich in form. "Like a swift horse at the yoke, he has been placed," [he says]; the yoke-pole (*dhūḥ*) is indeed the end, and this day is the end; this is the form of this day. "O Indra, this *arka* hymn praises you, the lord of treasures," [he says] with a verse containing the word "*arka*," thus it is rich in form.

"Place our glory high in heaven as if in the sky"—wherever speech devoted to the Brahman is uttered, there indeed his fame arises; wherever one who knows this concludes with this [verse], therefore one who knows this should conclude with this very [verse]. Thus ends the second section of the fifth chapter in the first Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka.

"We choose that of Savitṛ... and "O God Savitṛ, today for us..."—these are the opening and following verses of the Vaiśvadeva litany, belonging to the one-day sacrifice (*aikāhika*) and rich in form. Indeed, on this day, many various prohibitions are observed; it is for the sake of peace (*śānti*). The one-day sacrifice is indeed peace and a firm foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*). Thus, they finally find their firm foundation in peace and in the foundation. He who knows this finds his foundation, as do those for whom the Hotṛ, knowing thus, recites this.

"Of that god Savitṛ, the desirable [gift] is great"—this is the Sāvitra verse; "great" is indeed the end, and this day ends here; thus it is the form of this day. "Which of these two is the first, which is the later?"—this is the Dyāvāpṛthivīya verse; it has a common ending (*samānodarka*), and this day has a common ending; thus it is the form of this day. "Born without a horse, without a rein, worthy of praise"—this is the Ārbhava hymn; "the chariot is three-wheeled"—in this phrase there is the "threefold" (*trivat*); "threefold" is indeed the end, and this day ends here; thus it is the form of this day.

"Of this lovely, grey-haired Hotṛ"—this is the Vaiśvadeva hymn; it is multiform, for such is the form of this day. It ends with "The tawny one has lowed, fashioning the waters. The Vaiśvadeva Nivid-insertion is "May our auspicious intentions come from every side"; it belongs to the one-day sacrifice (*aikāhika*) and is perfect in its form.

"Much indeed is performed on this day, various kinds of warding-off; it is for the sake of peace. Peace is indeed the foundation, and the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) is the foundation. Thus, they finally find firm support in peace and in the foundation. He who knows this finds firm support, as do those for whom the Hotṛ, knowing thus, recites this. 'To Vaiśvānara, the supporter, the increaser of Truth'—this is the opening verse (*pratipad*) of the *Āgnimāruta* hymn. Support is indeed the end, and this day is the end; this is the form of this day."

"O Maruts, swift to sacrifice, with gleaming spears"—this is the hymn to the Maruts, which has a recurring finale; for this day indeed has a recurring finale, and that is the form of this day. "For Jātavedas let us press the Soma"—this *jātavedasyā* verse he recites before the hymn; the *jātavedasyā* is indeed a means of securing well-being (*svastyayana*), so he thereby effects well-being for the sake of safety.

"‘This hymn of praise for the worthy Jātavedas’—this [verse] belongs to Jātavedas; it has a common refrain (*samānodarka*). Indeed, this day has a common refrain, and that is the form of this day. Thus ends the third section of the fifth chapter in the first *Āraṇyaka* of the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa*. Thus ends the fifth chapter in the first *Āraṇyaka* of the *Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyakakāṇḍa*. Thus ends the first *Āraṇyaka* of the *Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyakakāṇḍa*.

Now begins the second Āraṇyaka. First Chapter. First Section. "This is the path; this is the action; this is the Brahman; this is the truth. Therefore, one should not be negligent, nor should one overstep it. For those of old who overstepped did not succeed; indeed, they came to ruin. This was said by the Seer: "Three generations have passed away; others have entered around the light. The Great One has taken its stand within the worlds; the Purifying One has entered the quarters."* *The reference is to the Ṛgveda 8.6.30. The "three generations" are interpreted as the past, present, and future, or as the three worlds. The "Great One" (Bṛhat) is the Sun, and the "Purifying One" (Pavamāna) is the Wind. The meaning is that while these cosmic powers abide, the seeker must remain on the path of truth.

"Three generations have passed beyond this"—those three generations that indeed passed beyond this are these birds, the Vaṅgas, the Vaṅgahas, and the Cerapādas. "Others have settled around the *arka* (flame)"—these generations have settled around this very *arka*, namely this Agni. "The Great One has stood within the worlds"—this very Great One who stands within the worlds is yonder Āditya.

"Pavamāna has entered the bay-colored quarters"—Pavamāna is indeed Vāyu, and he has entered the quarters, which are the bay-colored ones. Thus ends the first section of the first chapter in the second Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.

"For from the earth indeed all this arises, whatever there is here. Of that [earth], fire is the *arka*, food is the *aśītayaḥ*; for by means of food, all this attains (*aśnute*). "The intermediate space itself is the *uktha*"; for it is along the intermediate space that they fly, and along the intermediate space that they cause them to run. Of that [intermediate space], wind is the *arka*, food is the *aśītayaḥ*; for by means of food, all this attains.

"The sky itself is the *uktha*, for from that gift above, everything here—whatever exists—arises. Of that [sky], yonder sun is the *arka* (the food-eater), and food is the *aśītayaḥ*; for by means of food, this whole world consumes. Thus with respect to the deities; now with respect to the self (*adhyātma*). "The person (*puruṣa*) alone is the *uktha*. This very one is the Great Prajāpati. He should know: 'I am the *uktha*. His mouth is the *uktha*, just as the earth is [the *uktha*]. His speech is the *arka*, and food is the *aśītayaḥ*; for by means of food, this whole world consumes."

"The two nostrils are indeed the *uktha*, just as the intermediate space [is]. His breath is the *arka*; food is the *aśītayaḥ*, for by means of food one pervades all this. "That which is like the depression of the nose is the summit of the sun (*bradhna-viṣṭapa*). "The forehead is indeed the *uktha*, just as the sky [is]. His eye is the *arka*; food is the *aśītayaḥ*, for by means of food one pervades all this."

"The eightyfold similarity pertains both to the self (adhyātma) and to the divine (adhidaivata), for it is food alone [that constitutes this similarity]. By means of food, indeed, all these beings are made similar; by means of food one conquers this world, and by means of food that [other] world. Therefore, the eightyfold similarity pertains both to the self and to the divine, for it is food alone. "This very food is the eater of food (annāda). It is this earth alone, for from it everything that exists here arises—whatever there may be."

"Whatever indeed goes forth from here, that he eats entirely; whatever goes forth from there, this [earth] eats it all. She is this eater," so it begins. "The eater indeed becomes the one who eats. "He has no power over what he does not eat, nor over what they would not eat him. Thus ends the second section in the first chapter of the second Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.

Now, therefore, follows the creation of semen: Prajāpati’s semen is the gods; the semen of the gods is rain; the semen of rain is plants; the semen of plants is food; the semen of food is semen; the semen of semen is offspring; the semen of offspring is the heart; the semen of the heart is the mind; the semen of the mind is speech; the semen of speech is action. This performed action is this person, the world of Brahman. He consists of *irā* (nourishment); because he consists of *irā*, he is golden (*hiraṇmaya*).

"Indeed, he who knows this becomes golden in yonder world; he appears as golden to all beings. Thus ends the third section in the first chapter of the second Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka.

"Brahman entered this Puruṣa by means of his two fore-feet; because Brahman entered this Puruṣa by means of his two fore-feet, therefore they call them *prapade* (fore-feet), while others [call them] *śaphāḥ* (hooves) or *khurāḥ* (claws) in the case of other animals. "It glided upward from there; those became his two thighs (*ūrū*). "He said, 'Make it wide (*uru*) for me'; that became the belly (*udara*). "He said, 'Make it wide indeed for me'; that became the chest (*uras*)."

"The belly is Brahman"—thus do the Śārkarākṣyas worship; "The heart is Brahman"—thus do the Āruṇis [worship]. But he said, "They are indeed Brahman. It crept upward; it took hold of the head. Because it took hold of the head (*śiras*), it became the head (*śira*); that is why the head is called the head. These are the glories (*śriyaḥ*) resting upon the head: sight, hearing, mind, speech, and breath. Glories rest upon him who thus knows this "headness" of the head.

Competing with one another, they said, "I am the Uktha! I am the Uktha! Then they said, "Come, let us depart from this body; whichever of us, upon departing, causes this body to fall, that one shall be the Uktha."

Speech departed; it remained as before, eating and drinking, though not seeing or hearing. Sight departed; it remained as before, eating and drinking, though not seeing or hearing. Hearing departed; it remained as before, eating and drinking, though not seeing or hearing. Mind departed; it remained as before, eating and drinking, like one with eyes closed. Then the vital breath (prāṇa) departed; when the vital breath had departed, he fell down. Thereupon he was shattered; "he was shattered" (aśārīt), thus [it was called]; that became the body (śarīra); that is the essence of the body's being a body.

"Indeed, the hateful enemy and evil of one who knows this is shattered; his hateful enemy and evil are cast away. They [the vital breaths] did not injure one another, each thinking, "I am the *uktha*, I am the *uktha*. They said, "Come, let us enter this body again. Whichever among us, having entered it, causes this body to rise up—that shall be the *uktha*."

Speech entered [him], but he lay still; sight entered, but he lay still; hearing entered, but he lay still; mind entered, but he lay still; breath entered, and having entered into breath, he rose up. That became the Uktha. "This very Uktha is indeed breath," thus one should know that breath is the Uktha. The gods said to him: "You are the Uktha; you are all this; we are yours; you are ours."
This too has been stated by the Seer: "Thou art ours; we are thine. Thus ends the fourth section in the first chapter of the second Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.

The gods caused it to breathe; once breathed upon, it extended itself. Because it extended (*prātāyat*), that became the morning (*prātar*); because it came together (*samāgāt*), that became the evening (*sāyam*). Day is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*), and night is the in-breath (*apāna*). Speech is Agni; the eye is yonder sun; the mind is the moon; the ear is the quarters. This is the union of the dispatched [senses] with respect to the self (*adhyātma*); these deities are manifest there with respect to the divine (*adhidaivata*). This is what is meant by that statement.

"Knowing this, Hiraṇyadan Baida indeed said: 'No one has power over that which they would not give to me. For I know the sent-forth union established within the self; such indeed is that. "Truly, all beings bring tribute to him who knows this, for they have no power over him. That [syllable] *sat* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), *ti* is food (*anna*), and *yam* is yonder sun (*āditya*). This is threefold, for the eye is indeed threefold: white, black, and the pupil.

"Even if he should speak falsely, what he has uttered becomes truly real for him, who thus knows this reality of truth. Thus ends the fifth section in the first chapter of the second Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka.

"Speech is its thread, names are its cords; by means of this thread of speech and these cords of names, all this is bound together, for all this consists of names, and everything one addresses with speech. "Those who know this are indeed carried along, bound by the thread," it is said.

"His *uṣṇih* is the hair, his skin is the *gāyatrī*, his flesh is the *triṣṭubh*, his sinews are the *anuṣṭubh*, his bone is the *jagatī*, his marrow is the *paṅkti*, and his breath is the *bṛhatī*. He is covered by the meters (*chandas*); because he is covered by the meters, they are called 'meters' (*chandas*). Indeed, the meters protect him from evil action in whichever direction he may desire, for one who thus knows this 'meter-ness' (*chandastva*) of the meters. Thus it was said by the Seer (*ṛṣi*).

"I beheld the Herdsman"—this one is indeed the Herdsman, for he protects all this. "Not resting"—for he never lies down to sleep. "Moving hither and thither along his paths"—for he moves both hither and thither along his paths. "Clothing himself in convergent and divergent [rays]"—for he clothes himself in these very quarters, both convergent and divergent. "He revolves within the worlds"—for he revolves within the worlds.

"And further: 'Like wells covered by those who dig them,' for all this is indeed enveloped by the vital breath (prāṇa). This very space is supported by the Bṛhatī [metre] which is the vital breath; and just as this space is supported by the Bṛhatī which is the vital breath, even so should one know that all beings, down to the ants, are supported by the Bṛhatī which is the vital breath. Thus ends the sixth section in the first chapter of the second Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.

"Now, therefore, follow the manifestations (*vibhūti*) of this Puruṣa. Regarding this, it is said: "By his speech, the earth and fire were created; upon them the herbs are born, and fire makes them palatable, saying, 'Bring this! Bring that! Thus do these two—the earth and fire—serve their father, speech. "As far as the earth extends and as far as fire extends, so great becomes his world; his world does not decay as long as these two do not decay—the earth and the fire—for him who knows this manifestation of speech."

"Created by the vital breath (prāṇa) are both the intermediate space and the wind. Along the intermediate space they move; along the intermediate space they hear. The wind brings pleasant fragrance for him. Thus these two, the intermediate space and the wind, attend upon the vital breath as their father. As far as the intermediate space extends, and as far as the wind extends, so great becomes his world. His world does not decay as long as these two do not decay—the intermediate space and the wind—for one who thus knows this manifestation of the vital breath."

By the eye were created both heaven and the sun; heaven bestows rain and food upon him, and the sun provides light and illumination for him. Thus, these two—Heaven and the Sun—serve the eye as their father. As far as Heaven extends and as far as the Sun extends, so great becomes his world; his world does not decay as long as those two do not decay, for one who knows this manifestation of the eye regarding Heaven and the Sun.

The quarters and the moon were created from the ear. From the quarters comes this [sound] approaching him; from the quarters he hears distinctly. The moon distinguishes for him the bright and dark fortnights for the sake of meritorious action. Thus these—the quarters and the moon—serve the ear, their father. As far as the quarters extend, as far as the moon extends, so great becomes his world; his world does not decay as long as the world of these—the quarters and the moon—does not decay. This is the manifestation of the ear for one who knows it thus.

"Veda! [Thus it is said. Created by the mind are both the waters and Varuṇa; the waters bow down to him for meritorious action, and Varuṇa sustains his progeny through righteousness. In this way, the waters and Varuṇa serve the mind as their father. As far as the waters extend and as far as Varuṇa extends, so great becomes his world. His world does not decay as long as the worlds of these two—the waters and Varuṇa—do not decay—for one who thus knows this majesty of the mind.
Thus ends the seventh section in the first chapter of the second Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka.

"Āpa! Āpa!"—this [exclamation] refers to these very waters. This is the root; that is the top-knot. This is the father; these are the sons. For wherever there is the son, there is the father; and wherever there is the father, there is the son. This is what is being stated here. Knowing this, Mahidāsa Aitareya used to say: "I know myself from the gods, and I know the gods from me; for they are given from here, and they are gathered from here."

"This very mountain is sight, hearing, mind, speech, and breath; they call it the 'Brahma-mountain. He who knows this indeed swallows his hateful enemy and evil rival; his hateful enemy is utterly destroyed. This is the vital essence (*asu*), this is the breath (*prāṇa*), this is both prosperity (*bhūti*) and non-prosperity (*abhūti*). The gods worshipped it as 'prosperity' (*bhūti*), and so they became prosperous. Therefore even now, when one sleeps, one breathes out 'bhūḥ, bhūḥ.'"

"Those who say 'it is non-existence' are the Asuras; they were defeated. "He becomes [existent] by himself, and his hating enemy, his adversary, is defeated—he who knows thus. "This very one is both death and immortality. Regarding this, it was said by the Seer: "Moving away and moving forward, grasped by the *svadhā* (offering)," for by means of the out-breath (*apāna*), this in-breath (*prāṇa*) is restrained so that it does not go forth.

"The immortal one shares a common womb with the mortal"—for by this [statement] all this is of a common womb, for these bodies are mortal, while this deity is immortal. "Those two, eternal and moving in opposite directions, perceive each other; they do not perceive the other"—for indeed, these bodies perceive [the self], while this deity is immortal. He who knows thus becomes immortal in yonder world; he who knows thus becomes immortal, visible to all beings. Thus it is said. He who knows thus, he who knows thus.

Thus ends the eighth section in the first chapter of the second Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa. Thus ends the first chapter in the second Āraṇyaka of the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa.

Now begins the second chapter of the second Āraṇyaka; therein is the first section (the ninth): "This one who shines yonder worshipped this world in the form of a person. Verily, it was Prāṇa that worshipped it, for he who shines yonder is indeed Prāṇa. He worshipped it for a hundred years; therefore, the lifespan of a person is a hundred years. Because he worshipped it for a hundred years, they are called the Śatarcins; thus they call him who is truly [Prāṇa] by the name Śatarcins."

"He placed all this, whatever exists here, in the middle; because he placed all this, whatever exists here, in the middle, therefore they call him Mādhyama—him who is indeed such. Prāṇa is indeed Gṛtsa and apāna is Mada; because Prāṇa is Gṛtsa and apāna is Mada, therefore he is Gṛtsamada—him who is indeed such."

"This entire universe was his friend—whatever exists here. Because this entire universe was his friend—whatever exists here—he was Viśvāmitra; therefore, they call him Viśvāmitra, even though he is truly this [very one]. The gods said of him, "He indeed is the desirable (vāma) of us all. Because the gods said of him, "He indeed is the desirable of us all," he was Vāmadeva; therefore, they call him Vāmadeva, even though he is truly this [very one].

"He is indeed the Bṛhad-vāja. Vāja is offspring; he supports that offspring. Because he supports (bibharti), he is Bṛhad-vāja; therefore they call him Bṛhad-vāja, even though he is this very one. The gods said of him, "He is indeed the most excellent (vasiṣṭha) among us all. Because the gods said of him, "He is indeed the most excellent among us all," he is Vasiṣṭha; therefore they call him Vasiṣṭha, even though he is this very one.

"He has gone forward toward all this, whatever there is; because he has gone forward toward all this, whatever there is, therefore they call him *pragātha*, even though he is this very [Brahman]. "He has purified all this, whatever there is; because he has purified all this, whatever there is, therefore they call him *pāvamānī*, even though he is this very [Brahman]."

He said, "I shall become all this—both what is small and what is great. Therefore they became the *kṣudrasūktas* (the minor hymns) and the *mahāsūktas* (the major hymns); thus, though he is this very [Brahman], they call him the *kṣudrasūktas*, the *kṣudrasūktas*. And because he said, "Ah, I have spoken a *sūkta* (well-spoken word)," that became the *sūkta*; therefore it is called a *sūkta*, and thus they call him the *sūkta*, though he is this very [Brahman].

"This indeed is the *Ṛc*, for he shone (*arcata*) for all these beings; because he shone for all these beings, therefore he is called *Ṛc*—though he is this very [Self]. "This indeed is the *Ardharca* (half-verse), for he shone for all these halves; because he shone for all these halves, therefore he is called *Ardharca*—though he is this very [Self]."

"This indeed is the Foot (pada), for he has stepped upon (pādi) all these beings; because he has stepped upon all these beings, therefore it is called 'the Foot'—they call him by that name, though he is truly this [Brahman]. "This indeed is the Imperishable (akṣara), for he flows out from all these beings and they do not flow beyond him; because he flows out from all these beings and they do not flow beyond him, therefore it is called 'the Imperishable'—they call him by that name, though he is truly this [Brahman]."

All these ṛc-verses, all the Vedas, and all sounds are indeed this one single utterance (vyāhṛti), which is breath alone. One should know that "the ṛc is breath. Thus ends the second section of the second chapter of the second Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka.

"Indra sat down beside Viśvāmitra as he was about to recite this day. Having uttered the word 'food' (*anna*), he recited a thousand *bṛhatī* verses; by that, he attained Indra’s beloved abode. Indra said to him: "O Seer, you have indeed attained my beloved abode. O Seer, recite a second [thousand]. Having uttered the word 'food' once more, he recited a thousand *bṛhatī* verses; by that, he attained Indra’s beloved abode.

Indra said to him, "O Seer, you have indeed approached my beloved abode. O Seer, recite the third [part]. Having uttered the words "Food," he recited a thousand Bṛhatī verses; by that, he attained Indra's beloved abode. Thus it is said.

Indra said to him, "O seer, you have indeed come to my beloved abode; I grant you a boon. He replied, "May I know you alone. Indra said to him, "O seer, I am indeed the vital breath (prāṇa); you are the vital breath; all beings are the vital breath. For this vital breath is he who shines yonder. In this form, I am pervading all the quarters. My food is Mitra; my right side belongs to Viśvāmitra. I am truly he who shines yonder," he said.
Thus ends the third section in the second chapter of the second Āraṇyaka in the Āraṇyaka-section of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa. || 3 ||

"This very thousandfold *bṛhatī* has been perfected: its consonants are the body, its resonance is the self (*ātman*), its sibilants are the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Knowing this, Vasiṣṭha indeed became most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*) and thereby obtained that name. Indra taught this very thing to Viśvāmitra, and Indra taught this very thing to Bharadvāja; therefore, by virtue of that kinship, he is invoked in sacrifices.

This very Bṛhatī-thousand has thus been perfected; in that perfected Bṛhatī-thousand there are thirty-six thousand syllables, and there are just as many thousands of days in a hundred-year lifespan. By means of the consonants they obtain the nights, and by means of the vowels the days.

"This very thousandfold *bṛhatī* has been perfected. Of this very thousandfold *bṛhatī*, once perfected, he who knows thus—having become composed of wisdom (*prajñāmaya*), composed of the deities (*devatāmaya*), composed of Brahman (*brahmamaya*), and composed of immortality (*amṛtamaya*)—attains the deities. 'He who is I, that is He; he who is He, that am I. This was said by the Seer: 'The Sun is the Self of the moving and the stationary. One should indeed look upon this, one should look upon this."

Thus ends the fourth section in the second chapter of the second Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa. Thus ends the second chapter in the second Āraṇyaka of the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa.

"Verily, he who knows the fivefold Uktha as the Self—from which all this arises—is a possessor of true knowledge. Earth, wind, space, water, and light: this indeed is the fivefold Uktha as the Self, for from this all this arises, and into this it likewise dissolves. He who knows this becomes the refuge of his peers. Thus it is said.

"He who knows the food and the eater of food in that [pair] becomes an eater of food in this world, and food belongs to him. Water and earth are the food, for foods consist of these two; light and wind are the eater of food, for by means of these two all this food is eaten. Space is the receptacle, for in space all this is gathered together. He who knows thus becomes a receptacle for his peers."

"He who knows the food and the eater of food in that [world] becomes an eater of food in this world, and food belongs to him. Plants and trees are the food; the breath-bearers are the eater of food, for the breath-bearers eat the plants and trees. Among them, those which have teeth on both sides and are fashioned according to the form of man are the eaters of food; the other animals are the food. Therefore, they walk over the other animals as if they were mounted upon them, for the eater of food is mounted upon the food. He who knows this is born as one who is mounted over his equals."
Thus ends the first section of the third chapter of the second book in the Āraṇyaka-portion of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa. || 1 ||

"Of that [Self], he who knows it as most fully manifested attains it more fully. "The plants and trees, and whatever living beings there are—they know the Self as most fully manifested; for sap is seen in plants and trees, and consciousness in living beings. "But among living beings indeed the Self is most fully manifested; for in them both sap and consciousness are seen, whereas in others neither is seen."

"But in man alone is the Self more manifest; for he is most fully endowed with intelligence. He speaks what is known, he sees what is known; he knows what is to come; he knows the worlds and the non-worlds; being thus endowed, he seeks through mortal means the immortal. "But as for the other animals, their higher cognition consists only of hunger and thirst. They do not speak what is known, they do not see what is known, they do not know what is to come, nor do they know the worlds and the non-worlds. They are only as many [in capacity] as their intelligence allows, for their existence corresponds to their intelligence."
Thus ends the second section of the third chapter of the second Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa. || 2 ||

This very person is an ocean; he transcends the entire world—whatever he eats, he transcends it; if he eats the intermediate world, he transcends it; if he were to eat that world beyond, he would surely transcend it. This person consists of five elements: that which is his heat is light; those which are his apertures are space; then, that which is his blood, phlegm, and semen are water; that which is his body is earth; and that which is his breath is wind.

This very wind is fivefold: prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna. These deities are established within prāṇa and apāna alone—namely, sight, hearing, mind, and speech—for they merge back into prāṇa upon its departure.

This sacrifice is indeed the progressive sequence of speech and mind; this sacrifice is fivefold: the Agnihotra, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Four-Monthly sacrifices, the Animal sacrifice, and the Soma sacrifice. Of these sacrifices, the Soma sacrifice is the most perfect, for within it these five forms are found: that which precedes the pressings is one form, the three pressings themselves are [the next] three, and that which follows them is the fifth. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the third section of the third chapter in the second Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-kāṇḍa. || 3 ||

"He who indeed knows the sacrifice within the sacrifice, the day within the day, and the deity within the deities—he truly understands. This sacrifice within the sacrifice, the day within the day, and the deity within the deities is this Great Hymn (Mahaduktha).

This [Great Hymn] is fivefold by way of its Stomas: the *Trivṛt*, the *Pañcadaśa*, the *Saptadaśa*, the *Ekaviṃśa*, and the *Pañcaviṃśa*. By way of the Sāmans: the *Gāyatra*, the *Rathantara*, the *Bṛhat*, the *Bhadra*, and the *Rājana*. By way of the Metres: the *Gāyatrī*, the *Uṣṇih*, the *Bṛhatī*, the *Triṣṭubh*, and the *Dvipadā*. Its designation is: the Head, the Right Wing, the Left Wing, the Tail, and the Body.

"He chants the *prastāva* five times, he sings the *udgītha* five times, he performs the *pratihāra* five times, he intones the *upadrava* five times, and they reach the *nidhana* five times; thus it becomes a thousand *stobha*s. For in this way these five divisions (*vidhā*) are praised: that which precedes the eighty triplets (*tṛca-śīti*) is one division; the three sets of eighty triplets [themselves] constitute [the next three]; and that which follows is the fifth.

That thousand is all this; those "ten tens" are indeed all this, for such is the extent of number: ten tens make a hundred, and ten hundreds make a thousand; that thousand is all this. These are the three meters, for this food is prepared in a threefold way—eating, drinking, and chewing—and he obtains it by means of these. Thus ends the fourth section of the third chapter of the second Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka.

Regarding this, some recognize a thousand [verses] in various meters, thinking, "What else is real? What else shall we say?"—some [recognize] a thousand *triṣṭubh*s, some a thousand *jagatī*s, and some a thousand *anuṣṭubh*s. This has been stated by the Seer: "The sages perceived Indra, who was moving along the *anuṣṭubh*. This means that they perceived the vital breath (*prāṇa*) belonging to Indra within speech; this is what is expressed there. He indeed becomes capable of being glorious and possessed of auspicious fame.

"One who departs before the full span of life, it is said, does not attain completion, for this self is incomplete when one lacks speech, breath, or mind; for one who is being carried away does not experience through speech. One should bring [the hymn] to the *bṛhatī* meter, for the *bṛhatī* is indeed the complete self. This self is surrounded on all sides by bodies; just as this self is surrounded on all sides by bodies, even so is the *bṛhatī* surrounded on all sides by meters.

"For the self (*ātman*) is the middle among these limbs, and the *bṛhatī* is the middle among the meters. "He is capable of becoming illustrious and of having auspicious fame, but he is also capable of departing before his full span of life," so it has been said; "for this *bṛhatī* is the complete self; therefore, one should bring [the chant] into correspondence with the *bṛhatī* alone. Thus ends the fifth section of the third chapter of the second Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa Āraṇyaka-kāṇḍa.

This very *bṛhatī*-thousand, when completed, consists of eleven hundred and twenty-five *anuṣṭubh*s. Indeed, the less is taken up by the more. Regarding this, it was said by the Seer: "I [take] Vāc, the eight-footed," for there are eight syllables of four [each]; "the nine-cornered," for the *bṛhatī*, being completed, becomes nine-cornered; "touching the Truth," for Speech is indeed touched by the *ṛc* as Truth.

"From Indra, [I take] my body," he says. Thus, because this thousand Bṛhatīs becomes perfected as an Anuṣṭubh, therefore from that breath belonging to Indra, he constructs for the Bṛhatī its body, speech, in the form of the Anuṣṭubh. This indeed is the supreme transformation of speech, namely this Great Hymn (Mahaduktha); it is fivefold: the measured, the unmeasured, tone, truth, and falsehood.

"The Ṛg-verses are the *kumbyā* (the root), and that which is measured by them is the *yajus*; the *nigada* is speech uttered in vain, and that which is unmeasured is the *sāman*. Now, whatever is sung is the tone; 'Om' is truth, and 'no' is falsehood. This truth is the flower and the fruit of speech. He who speaks the truth is capable of becoming illustrious and of having a glorious reputation, for truth is indeed the flower and the fruit of speech."

"Now, this is the root of speech, namely untruth. Just as a tree whose roots are exposed withers and perishes, even so one who speaks untruth makes himself rootless; he withers and perishes. Therefore, one should not speak untruth; rather, one should show compassion by means of it. "Indeed, this syllable 'Oṃ' is turned away and empty. Whatever one says while saying 'Oṃ', all that is left behind for him. If he were to make everything 'Oṃ', he would leave himself empty; he would not be capable of fulfilling his desires."

"Now, this [syllable] *na* is complete with respect to the self. If one were to say 'no' to everything, evil reputation would arise for him, and that very reputation would destroy him right there. Therefore, one should give at the proper time and not give at the improper time; thus he unites truth and falsehood. From their union, offspring is born, and he becomes greater. Verily, he who knows that speech of which this [syllable *na*] is a modification—he is a knower of the correspondence (*saṃprativit*). The syllable *a* is indeed all speech; it becomes manifold and of various forms when manifested by the consonants (*sparśa*) and the sibilants (*ūṣman*)."

That which is whispered is his breath; and that which is loud is his body. Therefore, that [whispered part] is as if hidden, for what is bodiless is hidden, and breath is indeed bodiless.
