But that which is loud is the body; therefore, that is manifest, for the body is manifest. Thus ends the sixth section of the third chapter of the second Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-kāṇḍa.

This very thousand-fold *bṛhatī* has been perfected; it is glory, it is Indra, it is the overlord of beings. He who knows this Indra as the overlord of beings departs from this world with his vital strength intact—so said Mahidāsa Aitareya. "Having departed, having become Indra, he reigns in these worlds. Regarding this they ask: "If he attains that world in this form, then in what form does he return to this world?"

Now, that which is the blood in a woman is the form of Agni; therefore, one should not feel loathing for it. And that which is the semen in a man is the form of Āditya; therefore, one should not feel loathing for it. This Self (the man) bestows this self upon that Self (the woman), and that Self (the woman) bestows that self upon this self (the man). Thus they two come together with each other. By means of this form, he comes together with that world; by means of that form, he comes to this world. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the seventh section in the third chapter of the second Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa Āraṇyaka-kāṇḍa.

Regarding this, there are these verses (3): "That imperishable which the fivefold imperishable approaches, toward which the yoked ones, being yoked, drive together; that which is joined according to the Truth of truth—there all the gods become one. "That from which the imperishable proceeds as it is yoked, toward which the yoked ones, being yoked, drive together; hear about that which is joined according to the Truth of truth—there all the gods become one. "That of speech which is 'Om,' and that which is 'No,' and whatever of it is harsh, and whatever is excessive."

"Having separated that, the seers found it; they were satisfied with the name dependent upon the curd. In that wherein the name was satisfied with the curd, there the gods become all-yoked. Having struck away evil by means of that Brahman, the knower attains the heavenly world. No one speaks of him as "woman" by using the word *vāc* (speech), nor does anyone speak of him as "neither-woman-nor-man," nor does anyone speaking speak of him as "man. *Aḥ* is Brahman; therein he has arrived, saying "I am."

"This thousand-fold Bṛhatī, when perfected, consists of thirty-six thousand syllables; there are as many thousands of days in a human lifespan. By means of the living syllable one obtains the living day, and by the living day the living syllable. "It is free from desire and death, and it is the chariot of the gods. Speech is its pole, the two ears are its side-pieces, the two eyes are the yoked [steeds], the mind is the charioteer, and this vital breath (prāṇa) stands over it."

Thus it was said by the Seer: "Come hither with that which is swifter than thought, swifter even than the twinkling of an eye—swifter, swifter! Thus ends the eighth section in the third chapter of the second Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa. Thus ends the third chapter in the second Āraṇyaka of the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa.

Now begins the fourth chapter of the second Āraṇyaka; therein is the first section (the twenty-first): "In the beginning, indeed, this was the Self alone, one only; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking. He thought: 'Let me now create the worlds. He created these worlds: Ambhas, Marīcis, Mara, and Āpas. That which is beyond the sky is Ambhas; the sky is its support; the intermediate space is the Marīcis; the earth is Mara; and those that are below are the Āpas."

He reflected: "These worlds exist; now let me create the guardians of the worlds. He drew forth a person from his own body and brought him to life. He brooded over him; as he was being brooded over, his mouth burst open like an egg. From the mouth came speech, and from speech, fire. His nostrils burst open; from the nostrils came breath, and from breath, wind. His eyes burst open; from the eyes came sight, and from sight, the sun. His ears burst open; from the ears came hearing, and from hearing, the quarters of space. His skin burst open; from the skin came the body hairs.

From the body hairs, the plants and trees were produced; the heart was cleaved open, from the heart the mind, and from the mind the moon; the navel was cleaved open, from the navel the downward breath (*apāna*), and from the downward breath death; the generative organ was cleaved open, from the generative organ semen, and from the semen the waters. Thus ends the first section of the fourth chapter in the second *Āraṇyaka* of the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa*.

These deities, once created, fell into this great ocean; he overwhelmed them with hunger and thirst. They said to him, "Find for us an abode wherein, being established, we may eat food. He brought a cow to them; they said, "This is not sufficient for us. He brought a horse to them; they said, "This is not sufficient for us. He brought a human being to them; they said, "Ah, this is well done! Indeed, a human being is what is well done.

He said to them, "Enter according to your respective abodes. Fire, becoming speech, entered the mouth; Vāyu, becoming breath, entered the nostrils; Āditya, becoming sight, entered the eyes; the quarters, becoming hearing, entered the ears; the herbs and trees, becoming body hair, entered the skin; the Moon, becoming mind, entered the heart; Death, becoming the out-breath (apāna), entered the navel; and the Waters, becoming semen, entered the generative organ.

Darkness and hunger and thirst said, "Provide for us as well. He said to them, "I shall assign you a share among these very deities; I shall make you sharers therein. Therefore, for whatever deity an oblation is taken, hunger and thirst become sharers in it. Thus ends the second section of the fourth chapter of the second Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa. || 2 ||

He considered: "Now here are these worlds and the guardians of the worlds; let me create food for them. He brooded over the waters, and from those waters thus brooded upon, a form was born. That form which was born is indeed food.

When it was thus created, it sought to strike away [the eater] from the front. He sought to seize it with speech; he was not able to seize it with speech. For had he seized it with speech, one would have been satisfied merely by uttering the word "food. He sought to seize it with breath; he was not able to seize it with breath. For had he seized it with breath, one would have been satisfied merely by breathing toward it. He sought to seize it with the eye; he was not able to seize it with the eye. For had he seized it with the eye, one would have been satisfied merely by seeing it.

He would indeed have been satisfied with food had he been able to grasp it with the ear; but he could not grasp it with the ear. For if he had grasped it with the ear, he would have been satisfied with food after merely hearing it. He desired to grasp it with the skin; but he could not grasp it with the skin. For if he had grasped it with the skin, he would have been satisfied with food after merely touching it. He desired to grasp it with the mind; but he could not grasp it with the mind. For if he had grasped it with the mind, he would have been satisfied with food after merely thinking of it.

"He would surely have swallowed the food; he sought to seize it with his penis, but he was not able to grasp it with his penis. Had he grasped it with his penis, he would surely have emitted the food after swallowing it. He sought to seize it with his breath (apāna), and he swallowed it. Thus, this Vāyu is the seizer of food; for Vāyu is indeed the life of food. He reflected, "How indeed might this exist without me? He reflected, "By which way shall I enter?"

He reflected: "If it is spoken by speech, if it is breathed by breath, if it is seen by the eye, if it is heard by the ear, if it is touched by the skin, if it is thought by the mind, if it is exhaled by the out-breath, if it is emitted by the organ of generation—then who am I? He split open this very crown of the head and entered through that door. This is the door called "the Splitting," and this is the place of bliss (*nāndana*).

"He has three abodes and three states of sleep: 'This is an abode, this is an abode, this is an abode. Having been born, he looked upon all beings, thinking, "What else here could I possibly speak? He beheld this very person as the most pervasive Brahman. "I have seen this!"—therefore his name is *Idandra*. Indeed, his name is *Idandra*, yet they call him *Indra* cryptically; for the gods love the cryptic, for the gods love the cryptic.

Thus ends the third section of the fourth chapter in the second Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the second Āraṇyaka of the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa.

"Verily, this embryo first exists in man as this semen," so it is said. "This [semen], a concentrated radiance drawn from all his limbs, carries itself within himself; when he pours it into a woman, then he generates it—this is its first birth. Then it attains the state of being the self of the woman, just like her own limb; therefore, it does not harm her.

She contemplates this self of his as having entered therein; she, the contemplator, becomes the object of contemplation. Thus, the woman bears him in her womb, and he, even before birth, contemplates the boy after his birth. In that he contemplates the boy after his birth, he contemplates his own self. This is for the sake of the continuity of these worlds, for thus are these worlds continuous. That is his second birth.

"Thus this self of his is assigned to meritorious deeds; then this other self of his, having accomplished its purpose and reached the end of its lifespan, departs. Departing from here, he is born again; that is his third birth. This was said by the Seer: "While still in the womb, I indeed knew all the generations of these gods. A hundred iron fortresses confined me; then, like a hawk, I flew forth with speed."

"While still lying in the womb, Vāmadeva spoke thus. Knowing this, he, having ascended upwards after the dissolution of this body, having attained all desires in that heavenly world, became immortal—he became immortal. Thus ends the first section of the fifth chapter in the second *Āraṇyaka* of the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa*. Thus ends the fifth chapter in the second *Āraṇyaka* of the *Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa*.
Now begins the sixth chapter of the second Āraṇyaka; therein is the first section (the twenty-fifth):

"Which is this Self that we worship? Which one is that Self? [It is] that by which one sees, or by which one hears, or by which one smells odors, or by which one articulates speech, or by which one distinguishes between the savory and the unsavory. That which is this heart and mind—this is perception, comprehension, discernment, wisdom, intelligence, vision, steadfastness, thought, reflection, speed, memory, volition, resolve, life-force, desire, and will.

All these are indeed names of consciousness (*prajñāna*). This is Brahman; this is Indra; this is Prajāpati; these are all the gods; and these five great elements—earth, wind, space, water, and light—and these other things, small and mixed like seeds, whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from sweat, or born from sprouts; horses, cattle, humans, elephants; whatever here exists that is living, whether moving or flying, or stationary—all this.

"Consciousness is its eye. "The world is established in consciousness; consciousness is the eye of the world; consciousness is the foundation. "Consciousness is Brahman. By means of this conscious self, having departed from this world and having attained all desires in that heavenly world, he became immortal—he became immortal. Thus ends the first section of the sixth chapter in the second Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the second Āraṇyaka of the Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa.

"May my speech be established in my mind; may my mind be established in my speech. Be manifest to me. You two are the leaders of the Veda; do not abandon my learning. By this study, I join together day and night. I shall speak the Ṛta; I shall speak the Truth. May that protect me; may it protect the speaker. May it protect me; may it protect the speaker; may it protect the speaker. Thus ends the first section of the seventh chapter in the second Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the second Āraṇyaka of the Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa. Thus ends the second Āraṇyaka in the Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa.

Now begins the third Āraṇyaka. First Chapter. First Section. "Now, therefore, follows the Upaniṣad of the Saṃhitā. "The earth is the prior form, the sky is the subsequent form, and the wind is the conjunction (saṃhitā)," so said Māṇḍūkeya. "Space is the conjunction," thus Mākṣavya made known. He thought himself not fully refuted, saying, "He has not equaled me in this, my son. Āgastya said, "In that he was indeed refuted; for these two, wind and space, are indeed the same. This is with respect to the deities (*adhidaivata*); now with respect to the self (*adhyātma*).

"Speech is the prior form, mind is the subsequent form, and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the *saṃhitā*," said Śūravīra Māṇḍūkeya. Then his eldest son said to him: "Mind is the prior form, speech is the subsequent form; for one first forms a mental intention with the mind and then speaks with speech. Therefore, mind alone is the prior form, speech is the subsequent form, but the vital breath alone is the *saṃhitā*. In this matter, the view of the father and the son is the same.

Now, as for Śākalya’s view: "The earth is the prior form, the sky is the subsequent form, rain is the junction, and Parjanya is the uniter. Moreover, even when it rains while holding back the powerful [wind] and joining day and night, they say, "Heaven and Earth have united. Thus far with respect to the divine; now with respect to the self.

"This person, indeed, is the entire egg. "It consists of two shells," they say. Of that [egg], this is the form of the earth and this is the form of the sky; between them is this space, just as there is that space between heaven and earth. In this very space, the vital breath (prāṇa) is dependent, just as the wind is dependent on that [outer] space. Just as those three lights exist, so too are these three lights within the person.

"As that divine sun is in the sky, so is this eye in the head; as that lightning is in the intermediate space, so is this heart in the self; as this fire is on the earth, so is this semen in the lap. Thus, having identified the entire world with the self, he said: "This is the form of the earth, this is the form of the sky. He who knows this *saṃhitā* (union) is united with offspring, cattle, fame, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and the heavenly world; he reaches a full span of life.
Thus ends the second section in the first chapter of the third Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka.

Now, therefore, follow the doctrines of the Nirbhujas: "The earth is the *nirbhuj* (the bent), the heaven is the *pratṛṇṇa* (the pierced), and that which is between the two is the intermediate space. Now, if someone should revile one who speaks thus of the *nirbhuj*, he should say to him: "He has fallen from the two lower stations. And if someone should revile one who speaks thus of the *pratṛṇṇa*, he should say to him: "He has fallen from the two higher stations. But for one who speaks of both as being between the two, there is no possibility of reviling him.

For that which turns away the joints is the form of the *nirbhujam*; then, that which articulates pure syllables is the *pratṛṇṇam*. Indeed, at the very beginning, both [forms] encompass both [modes]. "One desiring food should recite the *nirbhujam*; one desiring heaven, the *pratṛṇṇam*; one desiring both, [should recite] between both. Thus it is said.

Now, if another should revile him while he is speaking with the *nirbhuja* style, one should say to him: "You have offended against the earth as a deity; the earth as a deity shall harm you. If another should revile him while he is speaking with the *pratṛṇṇa* style, one should say to him: "You have offended against heaven as a deity; heaven as a deity shall harm you. And if another should revile him while he is speaking with both [styles] in between, one should say to him: "You have offended against the intermediate space as a deity; the intermediate space as a deity shall harm you. Thus it is said.

"But as for how one might speak to someone who does not speak, or to whom one speaks, it should be done in such a way that [the result] is near at hand. One should never address a Brāhmaṇa with anything other than what is auspicious; one should address a Brāhmaṇa only with words of great splendor. Yet, even when there is great splendor, one should not address a Brāhmaṇa [with pride]; rather, one should say, 'Homage be to the Brāhmaṇas,' so said Śūravīra Māṇḍūkeya. Thus ends the third section of the first chapter in the third Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa Āraṇyaka.

Now, therefore, follow these verbal responses: "One should know that the lineage is the vital breath (prāṇa). If someone should criticize this lineage of the vital breath, and one should think he is capable [of refuting him], one should say to him: "You think you can join together the lineage of the vital breath; you cannot join together the lineage of the vital breath for me! One should say to him: "The lineage of the vital breath will abandon you! But if one should think he is incapable, [thinking] "He wished to join together the lineage of the vital breath but was not able to join it," one should say to him: "The lineage of the vital breath will abandon you!"

But as for how one might speak while telling a story, one should speak so as to be close to the truth, whether the person addressed is speaking or not; however, one should never speak of anything other than what is beneficial to a Brāhmaṇa. One should speak of a Brāhmaṇa as being exceedingly glorious (*atidyumna*), yet one should not speak of a Brāhmaṇa even when he is not exceedingly glorious. "Let there be homage to the Brāhmaṇas," so said Śūravīra Māṇḍūkeya. Thus ends the fourth section in the first chapter of the third Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka.

Now, indeed, they say: "The mouth is open. The preceding syllable is the former form (*pūrvarūpa*), the following syllable is the latter form (*uttararūpa*); that space which lies between the former form and the latter form is *saṃhitā*. He who knows this *saṃhitā* thus is joined with offspring, cattle, fame, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and the heavenly world; he reaches a full lifespan.

"Now, we say that they have 'upturned mouths' (nirbhujavaktra)," so said the short Hrasva Māṇḍūkeya. "The preceding syllable is the former form (pūrvarūpa), the following syllable is the latter form (uttararūpa). That space between the former and latter forms by which one effects the junction (saṃdhi), by which one distinguishes vowel from non-vowel, and by which one divides the metrical measures (mātrā)—that is the *saṃhitā*."

"He who knows this *saṃhitā* thus is joined with offspring, cattle, fame, spiritual splendor (*brahmavarcasa*), and the heavenly world; he reaches his full span of life. Then his son, Madhyama Prātībodhīputra, said: "These syllables, indeed, without being drawn apart or made manifold, he pronounces according to their respective phonemes. That measure which lies between the preceding form and the succeeding form, making the junction known—that is the *sāman*. I consider the *sāman* alone to be the *saṃhitā*."

This too has been stated by the Seer: "O Bṛhaspati, others do not know that which is beyond the Sāman. He who thus knows this Saṃhitā is joined with offspring, cattle, fame, Vedic splendor, and the heavenly world; he reaches a full lifespan. Thus ends the fifth section in the first chapter of the third Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka.

"Tārkṣya says that the *saṃhitā* is joined by means of the forms of the *Bṛhat* and *Rathaṃtara*. Speech is indeed the form of the *Rathaṃtara*, and breath is that of the *Bṛhat*; by both speech and breath, the *saṃhitā* is truly joined. It is said that Tārkṣya guards the cows for a year according to this *upaniṣad*. It is said that Tārkṣya guards the cows for a year within this measure. And this has also been stated by the Seer."

"He who knows this conjunction (*saṃhitā*) in this way is joined with offspring, cattle, fame, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and the heavenly world; he reaches his full span of life. Kauṇṭharavya says: "Speech is conjoined with breath; breath with the purifying wind (*pavamāna*); the purifying wind with all the gods; all the gods with the heavenly world; and the heavenly world with Brahman. This is the conjunction of the lower and the higher."

"He who knows this lower-and-higher *saṃhitā* is joined, just as this *saṃhitā* is, with offspring, cattle, fame, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and the heavenly world. If he should speak out, whether prompted by another or for his own purpose, while speaking he should know: 'The *saṃhitā* has gone to heaven; it will be so for the learned gods. And so it shall eternally be."

"He who knows this *saṃhitā* thus is united with offspring, cattle, fame, spiritual splendor (*brahmavarcasa*), and the heavenly world; he reaches his full span of life. "The *saṃhitā* is speech," said Pañcālacaṇḍa. "By speech indeed the Vedas are joined together; by speech the meters; by speech they reconcile friends; by speech all beings [are joined]; moreover, speech alone is all this."

When one studies this or speaks it, then the breath is in speech and speech licks the breath; and when one is silent or sleeps, then speech is in the breath and the breath licks speech. Thus these two lick each other: speech is the mother and the breath is the son. This has also been stated by a seer: "The single bird, he entered the ocean; he gazes upon this entire world."

"With a mature mind I beheld him nearby; the mother licks him, and he licks the mother. He who knows this *saṃhitā* thus is joined with offspring, cattle, fame, spiritual splendor (*brahmavarcasa*), and the heavenly world; he reaches a full lifespan. Now, therefore, follows the *Prajāpati-saṃhitā*: the wife is the prior form, the husband is the subsequent form, the son is the junction, and procreation is the union. This indeed is the *Aditi-saṃhitā*.

"Aditi is indeed all this—whatever exists here: father, mother, son, and progeny. This too has been declared by the Seer: "Aditi is the mother, she is the father, she is the son. He who knows this *saṃhitā* thus is joined with offspring, cattle, fame, spiritual splendor, and the heavenly world; he attains a full lifespan, he attains a full lifespan.

Thus ends the sixth section in the first chapter of the third Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa. Thus ends the first chapter in the third Āraṇyaka in the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa.

"The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the backbone," said the elder Śākalya. "Just as all other beams are supported within the backbone of a house, even so, within this vital breath, the eye, the ear, the mind, the organs of speech, the body, and the entire self (*ātman*) are supported. Regarding this very self, Hrasva Māṇḍūkeya used to say: "The vital breath is its form of heat (*ūṣman*); the bones are its form of touch (*sparśa*); the marrow is its form of tone (*svara*); and flesh, blood, and that which is fourth, the semi-vowels (*antaḥsthā*), are its form."

"But this has been declared as a triad," he said. Of this very triad—of the bones, the marrow, and the joints—there are three hundred and sixty of one kind and three hundred and sixty of another; thus they become seven hundred and twenty. And indeed, there are seven hundred and twenty days and nights in a year. This very self (ātman) is equal to the day; it consists of sight, it consists of hearing, it consists of the meters, it consists of mind, and it consists of speech.

Then Kauṇṭharavya said: "There are three hundred and sixty syllables, three hundred and sixty *ūṣman* sounds, and three hundred and sixty conjunctions (*saṃdhi*). Those syllables which we have mentioned are the days; those *ūṣman* sounds which we have mentioned are the nights; and those conjunctions which we have mentioned are the junctions of the days and nights. This is with respect to the divine."

Now, with regard to the self (*adhyātma*): those syllables which we spoke of as pertaining to the deities (*adhidaivata*) are the bones with regard to the self; those *ūṣman* sounds which we spoke of as pertaining to the deities are the marrow with regard to the self. This marrow, indeed, is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in its true essence, for it is semen. Verily, without the vital breath, semen is not emitted; and were semen to be emitted without the vital breath, it would putrefy and could not come into being. Those joints which we spoke of as pertaining to the deities are the limbs (*parvan*) with regard to the self.

Of this very triad—the bones, the marrow, and the joints—there are five hundred and forty on one side and five hundred and forty on the other; that makes eighty thousand. Indeed, those who know the *arkalins* accomplish eighty thousand *bṛhatī* verses each day. This, then, is the measurement of the syllables: the self consisting of sight, consisting of hearing, consisting of the meters, consisting of mind, and consisting of speech.

He who thus knows this Self—which is the measure of the syllable, consisting of sight, consisting of hearing, consisting of the meters, consisting of mind, and consisting of speech—attains union with the syllables, their same form, and residence in the same world; he becomes possessed of sons and cattle, and reaches a full lifespan. Thus ends the second section in the second chapter of the third Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka.

"Bādhva said there are four persons: the person of the body (*śarīrapuruṣa*), the person of the meters (*chandaḥpuruṣa*), the person of the Vedas (*vedapuruṣa*), and the Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*). As for what we called the 'person of the body,' that which is this very self belonging to the body—its essence (*rasa*) is this bodiless self consisting of consciousness (*prajñātman*). As for what we called the 'person of the meters,' that is simply the traditional collection of syllables (*akṣarasamāmnāya*); its essence is the letter *A*."

Regarding that which we called the "Veda-Person" (vedapuruṣa)—he by whom one knows the Vedas, namely the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda—of him, this very Brahman is the essence (rasa). Therefore, one should appoint as Brahman-priest (brahmā) one who is most proficient in the Veda (brahmiṣṭha), whoever may perceive any flaw in the sacrifice. Regarding that which we called the "Great Person" (mahāpuruṣa)—he who, as the year (saṃvatsara), destroys some beings while bringing others into being through unity—of him, this sun (āditya) is the essence.

"One should know that this bodiless self consisting of intelligence and that [self] which is yonder sun are one and the same. Therefore, for every person, the sun becomes [manifest]. This too has been stated by the Seer: 'The brilliant host of the gods has risen, the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni. Sūrya, the soul of the moving and the stationary, has filled heaven, earth, and the intermediate space. Bādhva used to say: 'I consider this Saṃhitā, when it is being joined, to be in accordance with this [truth].'"

"For it is this very one that the Bahvṛcas investigate in the Great Hymn (mahad-uktha), this one the Adhvaryus in the fire, this one the Chandogas in the Mahāvrata; this one in the earth, this one in the sky, this one in the wind, this one in space, this one in the waters, this one in the herbs, this one in the trees, this one in the moon, this one in the stars, this one in all beings—it is this very one they call 'Brahman. This very Self is equal to the year, consisting of sight, consisting of hearing, consisting of the meters, consisting of mind, and consisting of speech."

He who thus proclaims to another this Self—which is equal to the year, consisting of sight, consisting of hearing, consisting of the meters, consisting of mind, and consisting of speech—[attains the world of the sun]. Thus ends the third section in the second chapter of the third Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.

"The Vedas become like milk that has already been milked for him; he has no share in what is subsequently recited, nor does he know the path of merit. This too was said by a seer: "He who has abandoned the companion who knows the truth—there is no share even in his speech for him. Even if he hears it, he hears it in vain, for he does not know the path of merit. Thus, what is meant is: "He has no share in what is subsequently recited, nor does he know the path of merit."

Therefore, knowing this, one should not pile the fire for another, nor should one praise with the Mahāvrata for another, nor should one recite this day’s portion for another. One may, however, recite it at will for one’s father or for one’s teacher; in that case, it is as if he has performed it for himself.

"We have said that this bodiless conscious self and that [self] in the sun are one and the same. When these two become separated, the sun appears like the moon; its rays do not manifest, the sky becomes red like madder, the anus is displaced, and its head smells like a crow’s nest. One should know: 'His self has departed; he will not live much longer.'"

Whatever he considers to be his duty, let him do that; let him recite the seven verses beginning with "What is near and what is far," the one verse beginning with "From the ancient seed," the six verses beginning with "Where the Brahman [is] while purifying," and the one verse beginning with "Him who is beyond the darkness. Furthermore, wherever the sun appears as if pierced, or where it might be seen like the nave of a chariot wheel, or if one should see a perforated shadow—in those cases too, one should know it to be exactly thus.

Furthermore, if one should see oneself in a mirror or in water with a distorted head or no head at all, or if two young girls should appear inverted or distorted, one should know that it is exactly the same [as death]. Furthermore, if one should close one's eyes and look away, and when opening them again, things appear as if they were falling down like small gourds, and when one no longer sees them, one should know that it is exactly the same [as death].

"Furthermore, if one should cover one's ears and listen, there is this sound like that of a blazing fire or the rattling of a chariot; when one does not hear it, then one should know it to be exactly thus. Furthermore, where fire appears as if blue, or as if one should see lightning in a cloud, or should not see lightning in a cloud, or should see rays of light as if in a great cloud—then one should know it to be exactly thus. Furthermore, where one should see the earth as if it were blazing—then one should know it to be exactly thus. These are the direct perceptions. Now, the dreams: [The text continues with descriptions of various dream visions.]

He sees a black man with black teeth; he kills him. A boar kills him. A monkey leaps upon him. A swift wind carries him away. Having eaten gold, he spits it out. He eats honey. He eats lotus stalks. He wears a single white lotus. He travels yoked with donkeys and boars. Wearing a garland of *nalada* grass, facing south, he drives a black cow with a black calf. Thus [it is said].

"If he should see any of these [omens], he should fast, cook a *sthālīpāka* of milk-rice (*pāyasa*), offer oblations with each verse of the *Rātrisūkta*, feed the Brahmins with other food, and then eat the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) himself. "He who is unheard from this, unapproached, unthought, unknown, unseen, uncomprehended, and uncommanded; who is the hearer, the thinker, the seer, the commander, the proclaimer, the comprehender, and the knower—the inner person within all beings—he, one should know, is my Self."
Thus ends the fourth section in the second chapter of the third Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-kāṇḍa.

Now, indeed, this is the secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of all speech; for all these are indeed the secret doctrines of all speech. Regarding this, they say as follows: the consonants (sparśas) are the form of the earth, the sibilants (ūṣmans) of the intermediate space, and the vowels (svaras) of heaven. The consonants are the form of fire, the sibilants of wind, and the vowels of the sun. The consonants are the form of the Ṛgveda, the sibilants of the Yajurveda, and the vowels of the Sāmaveda. The consonants are the form of the eye, the sibilants of the ear, and the vowels of the mind. The consonants are the form of the breath.

"The warmth belongs to the apāna, and the tones belong to the vyāna. Now, indeed, this [divine] lute is divine, and that which imitates it is the human lute. As its head is, so is the head of that one; as its belly is, so is its hollow (ambhaṇa); as its tongue is, so is its sounding-board (vādana); as its strings are, so are its fingers; as its tones are, so are its tones; as its touches (sparśas) are, so are its touches—for just as this one is...

"It has sound, it has a bridge; thus it has sound, it has a bridge. For just as this [earth] is covered with hairy skin, so too is that [vīṇā] covered with hairy skin. Indeed, in former times they used to cover vīṇās with hairy skin. He who knows this divine vīṇā becomes one whose face is heard of; his fame reaches the earth wherever noble speech is spoken, and people there know him.

Now, therefore, follows the essence of speech (*vāgrasa*). In whatever assembly one who is studying or speaking should not shine forth, there he should mutter this *ṛc*: "The lip is the cover, the teeth are the felloes; surrounded by them, the tongue is the wheel-rim. Ruling over all speech, may she make me eloquent here. This is the essence of speech. Thus ends the fifth section in the second chapter of the third Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa Āraṇyaka-kāṇḍa.

Then Kṛṣṇa Hārita indeed recited this Vedic Brāhmaṇa-like passage for him: "Prajāpati, having created the creatures, became exhausted; he restored himself by means of the meters (chandas). Because he restored himself by means of the meters, therefore it is called *saṃhitā*. Now, in this very *saṃhitā*, the letter *ṇ* is strength, the letter *ṣ* is breath, and [the rest] is the self."

"He who knows these two, the letter *ṇ* and the letter *ṣ*, as being joined together in the *ṛc*s, knows the *saṃhitā* as possessed of strength and possessed of breath; he should know it as 'longevity' (*āyuṣya*). If he should have a doubt, [thinking] 'Shall I pronounce it with the letter *ṇ*? or 'Shall I pronounce it without the letter *ṇ*?'—he should pronounce it precisely with the letter *ṇ*. [Thinking] 'Shall I pronounce it with the letter *ṣ*? or 'Shall I pronounce it without the letter *ṣ*?'—he should pronounce it precisely with the letter *ṣ*."

"Because we study the *ṛc* verses according to the *saṃhitā* and because we recite the *adhyāya* of Māṇḍūkeya, by that means the *ṇakāra* and *ṣakāra* have been attained for us," so said the short-lived Māṇḍūkeya. "But because we study the *ṛc* verses according to the *saṃhitā* and because we recite the *adhyāya* of Māṇḍūkeya, by that means the *ṇakāra* and *ṣakāra* have been attained for us," so said the elder Śākalya.

Knowing this, the Ṛṣis, the descendants of Kavaṣa, indeed said: "For what purpose shall we study? For what purpose shall we perform sacrifices? For we offer speech into breath, or breath into speech; for that which is the source is itself the place of dissolution. These *saṃhitās* one should not teach to one who is not a resident pupil, nor to one who has not lived [as a student] for a year, nor to one who does not speak [the truth], so say the teachers, the teachers.

Thus ends the sixth section in the second chapter of the third Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-kāṇḍa. Thus ends the second chapter in the third Āraṇyaka of the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-kāṇḍa. Thus ends the third Āraṇyaka of the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-kāṇḍa.

"O Maghavan, find it; find a path; declare the directions according to the praise. Bestow [wealth], O Lord of powers, O possessor of many riches, among the many. "With these aids, do thou, O wise one, make us mindful. O Indra, for our glory, grant us food; for indeed Śakra is so. "For wealth and for strength, O wielder of the thunderbolt, O most powerful wielder of the thunderbolt, you exert yourself. O most liberal wielder of the thunderbolt, you exert yourself; come hither, drink, and rejoice. "Find wealth and heroic power; become the lord of strengths according to our desires."

"O most generous wielder of the thunderbolt, you who are the mightiest of heroes, you are praised. "He who is the most generous among the wealthy, O wise one, lead us toward [prosperity]. Indra knows him; I praise that self-controlled Śakra. "Him we invoke for protection, the unconquered conqueror. May he carry us across our enemies—he whose will is desire, whose delight is the Great Truth (Bṛhat-Ṛta). "We invoke Indra for the winning of wealth, the unconquered conqueror. May he carry us across our enemies; may he carry us across our adversaries."

"O wielder of the stone, bestow upon us that favor of yours which was [yours] of old, O Vasu! O most powerful one, your bounty is praised; for the capable Lord rules. "Now indeed, O Lord, slayer of Vṛtra, we shall entrust this new [hymn] to you. Let us two speak together in the contests; he is the hero who goes among the cattle, the friend who is very gracious and free from duplicity. "Even so, indeed, even so, O Agni! "Even so, indeed, even so, O Indra! "Even so, indeed, even so, O Viṣṇu! "Even so, indeed, even so, O Pūṣan! "Even so, indeed, even so, O Gods!"

"Thus indeed is Śakra; for Śakra is the controller, according to his will. "He who [is] for the sake of wrath against wrath, for the sake of pride against pride. "Approach him at all times. "O Maghavan, find [it], O finder! Thus ends the first section of the first chapter of the fourth Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa Āraṇyaka-kāṇḍa. Thus ends the first chapter of the fourth Āraṇyaka in the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa Āraṇyaka-kāṇḍa.
Thus ends the fourth Āraṇyaka in the Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka section of the Bahvṛca. 4.

Now begins the fifth Āraṇyaka. First Chapter. First Section. Therein: "For the Mahāvrata, there are twenty-five *sāmidhenī* verses. "In the case of the twenty-one [verses], before the penultimate one, there are four [to be added] beginning with *samidhāgnim*. "A bull dedicated to Viśvakarman is to be sacrificed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). "The *ājya* and *prauga* [stotras] belong to the Viśvajit. "The *hotrā*s follow those of the Caturviṃśa [sacrifice]. "And the Brāhmaṇacchaṃsin should insert [the verses] beginning with *īṅkhayantīrapasyuvaḥ* at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*). "The midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina*) consists of [the verses] beginning with *tīvrasyābhivayaso asya pāhi*."

"Among the *trikadruka* [vessels], the buffalo [drank] the barley-mixed milk"—this is the *stotriya*. "O Indra, come to us from afar; for the Asura Dyaus bowed down before Indra"—from this follows the *anurūpa*: "For him, the food is placed in front. This is the expansion of the *Marutvatīya* [śastra] of the Caturviṃśa [day]: "O singer, my [gift] is accompanied by success; drink the Soma, O fierce one, for which you are the impeller. "With what splendor do they, of equal age and uniform appearance, [gather]? "Accompanied by the Maruts, Indra, the bull, for the joy [of battle]. "The fierce one was born for power, the swift one"—this is the *Marutvatīya*.

When the Marutvatīya offering has been concluded, the Hotṛ, having gone out by the unobstructed path, offers three oblations of clarified butter on the Āgnīdhrīya fire with a ladle made of Udumbara wood, [saying]: "May Indra favor me; may Bṛhaspati favor me; may Soma favor me; may the goddess Vāk favor me. May Mitra and Varuṇa protect me here; may Heaven and Earth protect me at the first invocation. May the Ādityas, all the gods, and the seven kings who have been consecrated with water, protect me."

"May Vāyu, Pūṣan, Varuṇa, Soma, Agni, and Sūrya with the constellations protect me here. "O Pitṛs, this entire world, and the Maruts, sons of Pṛśni, who sing beautiful hymns; those who have Agni as their tongue, or those who are worthy of sacrifice—may you gods, who are easily invoked, grant us protection."

On the south, at the *mārjālīya* shed, there are ten ladles (*sruc*), the last of which is used for the *caturgṛhīta* (fourfold-drawn) oblation; having first taken [the butter] and placed it to the north of the fire, from the time of the ritual distribution (*viharaṇa*) onwards, the *mārjālīya* remains awake at midday. Into that enclosed space he offers the oblation—either at its eastern door, or its northern door, or its northeast door—with the formulas: "May I be as unassailable as Agni; may I be as a good seat as the earth"; "May I be as unassailable as the atmosphere; may I be as invincible as the sky."

"May I be peerless like the sun; may I be born again like the moon. "May I be unprecedented like the mind; may I become a source of renown like the wind. "May I be my own master like the day; may I be beloved like the night. "May I be born again like cattle; may I be a pair like the rays of light. "May I be essence like water; may I be form like the plants. "May I be pervasive like food; may I be a source of power like the sacrifice."

"May I be like Brahmā in the world, like the Kṣatriya in splendors"—thus [he says]. "O Agni, may this assembly be yours"—thus [he says]. Here, "distribute it, let it flow"—these three verses are recited without a pause between them (*ananvṛcam*). Standing here, he worships the sun; when the sun has turned, having circumambulated it to the right, he worships with these very *svāhā*-utterances: "Come hither! O honey! O honey! Drink this strong pressed juice! O honey! O honey! Thus [he says].

He instructs the female attendants: "Three [should carry] full jars, six [should carry] empty ones. "Go around this hearth and the water-jar three times clockwise; striking your right thighs with your right hands, say: 'Come, indeed! This is honey! This is honey! Thus ends the first section of the first chapter of the fifth Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka.

"When the Stotra has been introduced, pour out [the water] threefold; then, at this point, pour the remainder on the Mārjālīya fire and within the altar. Having gone out around the fire to the right, standing in front of the sacrificial post (yūpa) facing west, he worships the head of the fire, saying: "Homage to thee, the Gāyatra; that which is thy head. Returning by the same way as he came, facing north, he worships the right wing, saying: "Homage to thee, the Rāthaṃtara; that which is thy right wing."

Having passed beyond the tail of the fire-altar by the western side, facing eastward, [he addresses] the northern wing with: "Homage to thee, the great one, which is thy northern wing. Behind [the altar], facing east toward the tail, [he addresses] the tail with: "Homage to thee, the auspicious one; that which is thy tail, that which is thy foundation. To the south of the tail, [he addresses] the body with: "Homage to thee, the royal one; that which is thy body. Thus ends the second section in the first chapter of the fifth Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka.

"As he creeps toward this sacrificial hall (sadas)," so [it is said]. "The swing (preṅkha) is prepared in front," so [it is said]. Having washed the two pillars, the ropes, and the carrying-pole (vīvadha), having brought them in by the ritual path (tīrtha), having gone around the north of the Āgnīdhrīya fire-shed, [he enters] the sadas by the eastern door, [passing] to the north of all the hearth-mounds (dhiṣṇya). The wooden parts of the swing are made of Udumbara wood, or of Palāśa wood, or a mixture of both. There are three planks, planed on both sides, or two; and there are as many needles (sūci) as there are planks.

"One span long, sloping eastward, with its ends grasped, and pointing northward, it is fixed together at both ends by two needles pointing eastward. Having driven in two pillars to the south and north, he places the carrying-pole across them on both sides of the Hotṛ’s seat, making it level with the mouth of the maker.

In the *kuṣṭhā* (notches), there are apertures for the swing (*preṅkha*). It is raised upwards by two ropes: by the southern one on the right side and by the northern one on the left. These two ropes made of *darbha* grass should be threefold on the left and right; they should be five *vyāyāmas* long and doubled at the carrying-pole (*vīvadha*). Having wound them three times clockwise and having formed an upward knot, he ties it with a *niṣṭarkya* knot. "They shake it around with branches or with bundles of grass (*bṛsī*) until it no longer trembles. This swing should be four finger-breadths above the ground, or the measure of a closed fist.

"To the south, it should be raised higher or level with the *dhiṣṇya* hearth, at a distance of one *pada*. Thus ends the third section in the first chapter of the fifth Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka.

When the swing has been set in place, the Hotṛ, grasping a lute made of udumbara wood with a hundred strings with both hands, raises it from below toward the north, just as one would handle a lute. He should support its upper part with the seven meters increasing by four syllables each, or with ten; [using the formulas]: "With the Gāyatrī meter I raise you; with the Uṣṇih meter I raise you; with the Anuṣṭubh meter I raise you; with the Bṛhatī meter I raise you; with the Paṅkti meter I raise you; with the Triṣṭubh meter I raise you; with the Jagatī meter I raise you; with the Vairāja meter I raise you; with the Dvaipada meter I raise you; with the Atichandas meter I raise you."

Having recited the *chandāṃsi*, he circumambulates the places and three times scrapes the *vāṇa* upward with a moist *audumbara* branch, complete with leaves, using its base; saying, "For out-breath (*prāṇa*) thee, for in-breath (*apāna*) thee, for diffused breath (*vyāna*) thee, I scrape. He should further say, "And for other desires as well, I scrape again. Then he hands it, along with the branch, to the *chandoga*s.

With the words, "To the beings thee," he places his two hands on the western half of the plank. With the words, "Swing along with the out-breath (prāṇa)," he swings the swing forward; with the words, "Swing along with the diffused breath (vyāna)," he swings it crosswise; with the words, "Swing along with the downward breath (apāna)," he swings it toward himself. He mutters, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. With the words, "For the out-breath thee," he swings it forward; with the words, "For the diffused breath thee," he swings it crosswise; with the words, "For the downward breath thee," he swings it toward himself.

"May the Vasus ascend you with the Gāyatrī metre; may I ascend after them," saying this, he places his two forearms upon the rear plank. Then he should take hold of the front plank with both hands as if he were about to leap up. He should touch the middle with his chin, or else the joint between the two planks.

"May the Rudras mount you with the Triṣṭubh metre; may I mount after them," he says as he shifts his right thigh. "May the Ādityas mount you with the Jagatī metre; may I mount after them," he says as he shifts his left thigh. "May the All-gods mount you with the Anuṣṭubh metre; may I mount after them," he says as he mounts [the chariot] himself.

"Afterwards, he places his right foot forward upon his own seat, then the left; if one becomes fatigued, he places the other foot down, and if the other becomes fatigued, he places that one down, but he should not place both feet on the ground at once. "The *hotṛ*-assistants ascend their seats of grass (*kūrca*), and the *brahman* and the *udgātṛ* ascend the *audumbara* throne-seat. "If anyone who has obligatory duties should wish to go away, having instructed a guardian, having descended toward the east, and having performed his business, he should ascend again in this very same manner, accompanied by the *ājapa* formula."
Thus ends the fourth section in the first chapter of the fifth Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka.

He instructs the Prastotṛ: "When three verses remain—whether they be two and a half or twelve and a half—of the twenty-five-fold hymn-form (pañcaviṃśa-stoma), announce the first *pratihāra*. Jātūkarṇya says, "He causes it to be announced when twelve and a half [verses] remain. He mutters [the formula] once it has been announced.

"You are Suparṇa, the Garuḍa. I shall speak this speech which speaks much, which will fall much, which will do much, which will gain much, which will do more than much, which goes to heaven, which speaks of heaven, which will fall into heaven, which will do heaven, which will gain heaven, which will carry this sacrifice to heaven, and which will carry me, the sacrificer, to heaven"—thus [he says]. The word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) applies only when one is initiated (*dīkṣita*), not when one is not initiated.

"One should say 'svaramum' for one who is dear to him, but one should not say 'vakṣyantīm'," so it is said. And [there are] the *ukthavīrya* formulas: "May my breath be united with speech; may I be united with speech; may my sight be united with the mind; may I be united with the mind; may my hearing be united with the self; may I be united with the self; in me be greatness; in me be splendor; in me be fortune; in me be enjoyment; in me be the *stobha*; in me be the hymn; in me be the verse; in me be the sound; in me be glory; in me be prosperity; in me be fame; in me be liberation. Having called out "Vāk," he mutters this.

"There are three *āhāva*s: for the *śastra* and so forth, for the *nivid*, and for the *paridhānīyā* verse. "The Adhvaryus cause these words to be uttered. "On this day, one should give abundant food. "The prince has a hide stretched [over him] and beats the ground-drum; the wives play the *kāṇḍavīṇā*; there is sexual intercourse between a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) and a wanton woman (*puṃścalī*); there is conversation between them; they chant the *niṣkevalya* with many *sāman*s; he begins with the *stotriya* verse of the *rājan* [sāman]."
Thus ends the fifth section in the first chapter of the fifth Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka.

"That indeed was the eldest among the worlds; that fame of yours, O Maghavan, has increased even further through your greatness for the sake of heroic power. You, the most manly among men, [we praise] with songs and hymns"—thus three [verses].

In this regard, some teachers say that one should remove these two lines—"O sweetest with sweetness, join the delights; conquer well with honey the honey"—from their place in the self and place them instead in the places of the wings, while the other two—"*O Indra, Maghavan, we who seek horses and prizes; O Indra, bestow on us the chariot-horse, the cow, and the prize*"—should occupy the place of those two. "Thus," they say, "one bestows glory upon oneself—the cow and the horse—and [bestows] both upon the wings for the sake of flight."

With this verse, "Like the roar of flowing waters," he interweaves these [verses] line by line; he places the *bṛhatī* form with the subsequent verses containing the word "roar" (*nada*), and in the first [verse], he inserts human syllables—one in each foot, except at the end of the third foot. Indeed, he thus performs the *vihāra*. To illustrate, we shall cite an example: *tad id āsa bhuvaneṣu jyeṣṭham |* *nadaṃ va odatīnām |* *yato jajña ugras tveṣa nṛmṇo ru |* *nadaṃ yoyuvatīno3m ||*

"Born at once, he overcomes his enemies; you are the lord of the inviolable cows. He whom all the protectors rejoice in—that one, O Soma, do thou seek for the sake of the milch-cows. Thus [he recites] this [verse] three times. If they were to chant with the *rājana* sāman while other [verses] have been prescribed, then those [prescribed verses] should be used here according to their proper place. If they were to chant while these [verses] have not been prescribed, then having extracted as many [verses] from what has been prescribed, he should recite them there, and these [unprescribed ones] right here. If they are among others [of the same class], they are [to be recited] before the *sūdadohas* verse.

"Tad id āsa" and so forth is the *śastra*; here the response (*pratigara*) is unextended (*avihṛta*). "Tā asya sūdadohasaḥ" and so forth is the *sūdadohas* [verse]; [the response is] "sūdadohāḥ, sūdadohāḥ. Thus ends the sixth section in the first chapter of the fifth Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa. Thus ends the first chapter of the fifth Āraṇyaka of the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa.

Now begins the second chapter of the fifth Āraṇyaka; therein is the first section (the seventh). "Whose this is—the dust-raising, impetuous, conquering, and powerful forest—Indra’s lofty and delightful [strength]. "No one has dared to overcome his daring power, which is itself bold; for long ago, Indra’s daring might was beyond all affliction. "May he grant us that wealth, that golden-hued treasure; Indra, the most powerful lord among men."

"Sūdadohas," thus [it is said]. "The head is the Gāyatra; 'Indramid gāthino bṛhat,'" thus [it is said]. If they should chant while other [verses] have been recited, there is a combination of both; there is no reversal if they should chant when [verses] have not been recited, nor when they are mixed. "Sūdadohas" is at the end of the hymn (sūkta). "Vijavaḥ. "Pressed for thee is the Soma; come to the sacrifice, rejoice, O Maghavan, in the exhilaration rich in boons; most liberal Indra, be praised as the one who bestows wealth. Thus [it is said].

"He and Saha have conquered the enemies in the slaying of Vṛtra; he is the one who penetrates as a vigorous hero. Let us magnify Indra, our leader. "The lord, the wealthy one, the gatherer, dwelling on the mountains; the impetuous one faces you both. Indra is to be invoked repeatedly by many with his own movements. "Sūdadohas. These three [verses] are the neck and the head; the *vijava* [sections] are the whole half-verse. Thus ends the first section of the second chapter of the fifth Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa Āraṇyaka-kāṇḍa.

"The *rathaṃtara* is the right wing. "We cry out to you, O hero; we cry out to you for the first draught"—these are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* *pragāthas* of the *rathaṃtara*; though they consist of four [verses], he makes them into six *bṛhatīs*.

"Of Indra, indeed, I shall proclaim the heroic deeds," "In thee, O Indra, even our fathers,"—these fifteen [verses]; "He who was born fierce as a sharp-horned bull, formidable, mighty, for heroism, self-dependent," "The sacred words have been raised up through desire for glory," "Great is your Indra, surpassing the fierce,"—these five hymns; "O Indra, come to us from afar, come to us from near," is the *saṃpāta*; "For thus indeed the Soma is exhilarating," is the *paṅkti* and the *sūdadohas*. Thus the latter [section] is in the Bṛhatī meter.

"Tvāmid dhi havāmahe, tvaṃ hy ehi cerave"—these two *pragāthas* serve as the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* for the *bṛhatī* verses; though there are four [verses], he makes them six *bṛhatīs*. "Tamu ṣṭuhi yo abhibhūtyojāḥ," "Suta it tvaṃ nimitra indra soma," and "Abhūr eko rayipate rayīṇām"—these are eight hymns; "Kathā mahām avṛdhat kasya hotuḥ" is the *saṃpāta*; "Indro madāya vāvṛdhe" is the *paṅkti*; and [the verse] "sūdadohas" [is added].

"The *rathaṃtara* [sāman] is the right wing, the *pañcadaśa* stoma, one hundred [verses], the *vasiṣṭhaprāsāha*, and the *bārhata*; the *saptadaśa* stoma, two hundred [verses], and the *bharadvājaprāsāha* is the left wing. 'The auspicious tail is among the *dvipadā* verses'—these nine [verses] beginning with 'imā nu kaṃ bhuvanā sīṣadhāma' and 'āyāhi vanasā saha' are recited; then there are those not recited: 'pra va indrāya vṛtrahantamāya viprā gāthaṃ gāyata yajjujoṣat'."

"The gods worship the Sun as the one worthy of praise; he is the celebrated youth who thunders—this is Indra. "Dwelling near the honey-sweet food, prospering, we meditate upon that wealth, O Indra. "O giver, from every side bring to us from every side that which we beg of thee, O most powerful one. "O excellent leader, thou art the most manly, resplendent, and most bountiful for the winning of booty. "For thou alone rulest, ever unassailable by might."

"O wise one, you were the Prastobha of the universe, whether in the past or indeed here now. "O Mitra and Varuṇa, grant us nourishment; O Indra, make for us abundant and swelling food. "The Soma, seeking wealth, impels the auspicious step toward the gift; may wealth not touch the one who has no vow. "This is Brahman"—these are three verses. "Support him"—this is one verse. The *sūdadohas* [verse] is "When he has bellowed"; the *dhāyyā* is the *sūdadohas*.
Thus ends the second section of the second chapter in the fifth Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka.

"The *gāyatrī* triplet consists of eighty verses. From the hymn beginning with "Great is Indra by his might" (*māhā~ indro ya ojasā*), he extracts the last three verses; from the hymn beginning with "The *purolāśa* for us from the soma-juice" (*purolāśaṃ no andhasaḥ*) and "Indra alone is the drinker of soma" (*indra it somapā ekaḥ*), he extracts the last three verses of those; having extracted from them the verse "Sweet are the soma-draughts, come hither" (*svādavaḥ somā āyāhi*), he replaces it with the verse "For no other have I made strength" (*na hy anyaṃ balākaram*). He recites the single verse "Now that the hundred-fold lord was born" (*jajñāno nu śatakratuḥ*), and the remainder of the hymn begins with "The much-invoked, the much-praised" (*puruhūtaṃ puruṣṭutam*). Finally, he extracts the last verse, "He has raised up the famous wealth" (*udhed abhi śrutā magham*).

*prakṛtāny ṛjīṣiṇaḥ*, *ā ghā ye agnim indhate*, *ā tū na indra kṣumantam*—these hymns are the *sūdadohas*. Thus ends the third section in the second chapter of the fifth Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka.

The Bārhata *triṣṭubh* collection consists of eighty-three triplets (*ṛca*). From the verse "Mā cid anyad viśaṃsata" (Do not praise anything else), one removes one; from the twenty verses beginning with "Pibā sutasya rasinaḥ" (Drink of the pressed juice), one removes the seventh and the eighth; from the fourteen verses beginning with "Yad indra prāg apāk udak" (When, O Indra, [you go] east, west, north...); from the fifteen verses beginning with "Vayaṃ gha tvā sutāvantaḥ" (We, having pressed the juice for you...); and from the verse "Mo ṣu tvā vāghataś cana" (Not even the priests themselves...), one removes the two-footed (*dvipadā*) verse. Then there is the *pragātha* belonging to the *rathantara* melody. Now, having removed the *pragātha* beginning with "Nakiḥ sudāso ratham" (No one [stops] the chariot of Sudās...), there follows the verse "Tvām id dhyo naraḥ" (Only you, indeed, the men [invoke]...).

He places this *pragātha* as a response: "Abhipra vaḥ surādhasam. Then there are the six hymns of the Vālakhilyas beginning with "Yaḥ satrāhā vicarṣaṇiḥ. The remainder consists of the two hymns beginning with "Ayaṃ te astu haryataḥ" and "Ubhayaṃ śṛṇavacca naḥ," from which he omits both the seventh and the eighth verses. He omits the final verse of the hymn beginning with "Tarobhir vo vidadvasum. There are eleven verses beginning with "Yo rājā carṣaṇīnām," and nine verses beginning with "Taṃ vo dasmamṛtīṣaham" and "Ā no viśvā suhavyo yā indra bhuja ābhara."
"Sūdadohas. Thus ends the fourth section in the second chapter of the fifth Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa Āraṇyaka-kāṇḍa. || 4 ||

The eighty-three triplets are in the *auṣṇiha* meter. Regarding the hymn beginning with "O Indra, greatest drinker of Soma," one omits the last verse of the triplet beginning with "Sing forth toward him. From the hymn beginning with "Sing the *sāman* for Indra, O friends, let us invoke [him]," one omits the three final verses. Regarding the triplets beginning with "He alone who bestows wealth," "Come with the stones to the pressed [juice]," and "Whose [Soma] that Śambara [drank] in intoxication," these are *gāyatrī* verses; they become *uṣṇih* verses by way of completion. There are seven *gāyatrīs* and six *uṣṇih*s in each. Regarding the verses beginning with "If I, O Indra, as you are" and "Praise the sovereign of the peoples."

From the *sūkta* "vārtrahatyāya śavase," he omits the last two verses; from the *sūkta* "surūpakṛtnumūtaye," he omits the last three verses; from the *sūkta* "indrasānasiṃ rayim," he omits the last three verses beginning with "ya ānayat parāvataḥ"; and [he omits] the three verses beginning with "revatīr naḥ sadhamādaḥ," which are the *sūdadohas* verses. Thus, these thirty-eight triplets (*tṛca-aśītis*) are all to be recited half-verse by half-verse. These are the food-triplets (*anna-aśītis*). The *vaśa* verses are the belly.

"tvāvataḥ purūvaso" (O you who possess much wealth), "vaśaḥ sanitah su sanitah" (the controller, the winner, the good winner)—this is the end; "dadī rekṇaḥ" (he has given wealth)—this is a *dvipadā* (two-footed verse); "nūnam atha" (now indeed)—this is a *ekapadā* (one-footed verse); "tā asya sūdadohasaḥ" (those [waters] of his which yield the essence)—this is the end; the *sūdadohas* (essence-yielding) verses are thus repeated. Thus ends the fifth section of the second chapter of the Fifth Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa Āraṇyaka-kāṇḍa. Thus ends the second chapter of the Fifth Āraṇyaka in the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa Āraṇyaka-kāṇḍa.

"Ūrū," thus [it is said]. From the half-verse beginning "O Indra and Agni, you two indeed for us well... onwards, there is the Gāyatrī-form; for the subsequent [half-verse], there is the Anuṣṭubh-form until the penultimate verse. The insertion of the Nivid is at the verse "pra vo mahe mandamānāyāndhasaḥ. Between the verses "vanena vāyo nyadhāyi cākanyaḥ" and "jāta eva prathamo manasvān," the insertion consists of ten verses addressed to Indra, in Triṣṭubh and Jagatī meters, which result in Bṛhatī meters, including the verses "āyāhy arvāṅ upa vandhureṣṭhāḥ" and "vidhuṃ dadrāṇaṃ samane bahūnām."

As many nights as they may have spent [in the womb], for so many years of his life might he wish to live; year by year, decade by decade, or not at all. "That vigorous one, impelled by the gods, Indra, shines over all"—this is a single-footed verse. "Indra, all have magnified"—this is an Anuṣṭubh verse. Having recited the first half-verse of that [Anuṣṭubh], he interlocks it with the first half-verse of the next [verse] by means of the feet, foot by foot, in the manner of an Anuṣṭubh, until the penultimate verse.

He interlocks each subsequent half-verse with each preceding half-verse; the remainder is recited in its natural order. Having recited six verses beginning with "Drink the Soma, O Indra; let it exhilarate thee," and four verses of the hymn "A seat has been prepared for thee, O Indra," he concludes with the penultimate verse, having joined it to the final one. When the *uktha* has been concluded, he mutters the *ukthasaṃpad* formula. At the place of the *ukthavīrya*, the *ukthadoha* is performed.
Thus ends the first section of the third chapter in the fifth Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka. || 1 ||

You are the head of the worlds, the essence of speech, the splendor of breath, the abode of the mind, the resting place of the eye, the source of the ear, and the foundation of the heart—indeed, everything. You are Indra, the imperishable action, the immortal, the sky. You are the cosmic order (*ṛta*), the truth, the victorious, the arbiter of disputes, the end of speech, the pervasive one, the light higher than all, the upholder, the one beyond contradiction, the ancient, the all-encompassing speech, the far-reaching, the near-reaching, and the cow that overflows with water.

"The eye, the ear, the breath—measured by truth; speech abundant, mind pervasive, heart fierce; supporting the Brahmins, auspicious food, the purifier of the rains, the fortune of cattle, the highest on earth, most full of vigor like Varuṇa, having austerity as its body, Indra as its eldest, a thousand streams, ten thousand syllables—milking the immortal. These, indeed, are your prosperities of the *uktha*, these are the manifestations of speech. With these, milk for me here the great glory of immortality.

"Prajāpati created this Brahman, the essence of the Vedas. Through it, may I nourish the universe; may I milk all great desires. "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, you are the threefold Veda. Milk forth Brahman for me; milk forth progeny for me. "Milk forth life and breath for me; milk forth cattle and the people for me. Milk forth prosperity and fame for me. Milk forth the world, spiritual luster, fearlessness, and the success of the sacrifice for me. Thus he causes [the sacrificer] to recite, provided that he is not already aware [of the meaning].

"Recite the offering prayer for the Soma with the words *omukthaśā yaja*," being thus prompted for the sacrifice, he utters the *āgūr* formula "ye yajāmahe" and sacrifices with the standard [formula] alone; having separated [the portions], he pronounces the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*. Thus the recitation following the *vaṣaṭkāra* has been explained. The Adhvaryu brings forward the *ukthapātra* and the cups for the *atigrāhya* libations. Having signaled for the consumption, the Hotṛ descends from the swing toward the east.

Then they fasten this swing facing westward, so that it will not strike the one who is about to consume [the Soma] after he has recited the praise. For the Hotṛ consumes [the Soma] while seated upon the seat of the swing. Then the Hotṛ consumes this Ukthya-vessel with the muttered formula: "May the goddess Vāc be satisfied with the Soma! May King Soma rain down life for my vital breath. May that breath of mine yield all life, the great."

From the *ābhiplavika* [six-day period], the third pressing is different: [it consists of] the forty-one verses beginning with "Of this lovely, grey-haired Hotṛ" (*asya vāmasya palitasya hotuḥ*) from the *salila* hymn of Dairghatamas, the *ānobhadrīya*, and in its place, the *pratipad* and *anucara* of the Vaiśvadeva [śastra] belonging to the one-day sacrifice (*aikāhika*). Thus it is said.

If the *yajñāyajñīya* were to fail, [one should perform] the six *stotriya* verses beginning with "O Agni, yours is glory and vigor," as the *anurūpa*. If they should chant the *ilānda* in more than [the usual number of] verses, then the *anurūpa* consists of those beginning with "As we [serve] Agni with our own well-fashioned hymns. Thus the *mahāvrata* is completed; this day concludes as an *agniṣṭoma*. At the appropriate time, they should carry away the swing (*preṅkha*) for the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) and burn the grass mats (*bṛsī*). Thus ends the second section of the third chapter in the fifth Āraṇyaka of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.

"One who has not been initiated should not recite the *mahāvrata* hymn; nor in the absence of fire, nor to another person, nor before a year has passed—so say some. One may, however, recite it at will for one's father or for one's teacher, for in that case it is as if it were recited for oneself. Regarding the *hotṛ*-recitations, there is one direction (*praiṣa*): "O reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice to Soma! This applies whether the cups are *nārāśaṃsa* or not. For the *hotraka* priests, the direction is: "O reciter of the *uktha*, sacrifice to the Somas!"

"One should not teach this to one who is not a resident pupil, nor to one who has not resided for a year, nor indeed to one who has not resided for a year, nor to one who is not a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), nor to one who is not a student of sacred knowledge, nor indeed to one who is not a student of sacred knowledge, nor to one who has not reached this place. "It is not more than once; from saying it once or twice, it is exactly two-fold," so it is said. "One should teach it to each one individually," so Jātūkarṇya used to say. "Not to a calf, and not a third time," so it is said.

"One who is standing does not recite for one who is standing; one who is walking does not recite for one who is walking; one who is lying down does not recite for one who is lying down; one sitting above does not recite for one sitting above; nor one sitting below for one sitting below. "One should not study while leaning against something, nor while propped up, nor while being fanned, nor having placed his knees on a seat, nor with his feet raised unsupported, nor after eating meat, nor after seeing blood, nor after [seeing] a dead body, nor after stepping over anything impure, nor after applying oil, nor after anointing himself, nor after having a massage, nor after having a haircut by a barber, nor after bathing, nor after anointing himself with cosmetic unguents."

"Having put on a garland, one should not approach a woman, nor scratch oneself, nor scrape oneself," so it is said. "One should not complete this [study] on a single day," thus said Jātūkarṇya; "One should complete it," said Gālava; "One should certainly complete it before the eighty *ṛcas*," said Āgniveśyāyana; "Restraining oneself in different places for different [sections]," so it is said. Where one studies this, there one should study nothing else; but where one studies something else, there one may study this at will.

"One does not become a *snātaka* by not studying this, even if one has studied much else; indeed, one does not become a *snātaka* by not studying this. "One should never be negligent regarding this. "If one is not negligent regarding this, one should know: 'I have attained my goal. "One should know: 'Truth is sufficient. "One who knows this should not point out this [knowledge] to one who does not know it, nor should he eat with him, nor should he be a fellow-drinker with him."

Now, therefore, we shall explain the rules for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-dharma*). One should not study when the water in the armpits has not yet dried, nor in the forenoon when shadows have not yet converged, nor in the afternoon; nor when clouds are overhead outside the rainy season, nor during rain itself. One should not interrupt Vedic study for three nights [after such events], nor should one engage in conversation about it, nor should one recite it at night, nor even mention its name. "Tat" (That), indeed, is the name of this Great Being. He who knows its name thus becomes Brahman, he becomes Brahman.

Thus ends the third section (khaṇḍa) of the third chapter of the fifth Āraṇyaka in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa. Thus ends the third chapter of the fifth Āraṇyaka in the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa.

Oṃ! Having risen, I take up the luster of Śukra. That I place within myself. May sensory power come to me. In me be prosperity, in me be glory. May I be whole, possessed of breath and strength. I rise up; may prosperity follow me. May the deities rise up and follow me. Unimpaired is my sight, impelled is my mind. Sūrya is the best of lights; O consecration, do not harm me. That bright eye, established by the gods, rises upward. May we see for a hundred autumns; may we live for a hundred autumns.

O Agni, you are the guardian of vows, a god among mortals; you are to be praised at the sacrifices. Speaking, O Śakuni, utter auspicious words; sitting silently, take note of our good intention. When you fly up, you speak like a *karkuri* bird; may we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly. [I praise] the inexhaustible fountain with a hundred streams, the wise father of words, the joyous *meli* in the lap of his parents—O Heaven and Earth, protect him who speaks the truth.

May the Vāk (Speech) be established in my Manas; may my Manas be established in the Vāk. Be manifest before me. You two are the leaders of the Veda; do not abandon what I have heard. Through this study, I join together day and night. I shall speak the Ṛta; I shall speak the Satya. May that protect me; may it protect the speaker. May it protect me; may it protect the speaker; may it protect the speaker. *Oṃ*! Peace! Peace! Peace! Thus ends the Uttara-śānti. Thus concludes the fifth Āraṇyaka in the Brāhmaṇa-Āraṇyaka-Kāṇḍa of the Ṛgveda.
